questions.prompt:
For each feature, state whether it is found in DNA only, mRNA only, both DNA and mRNA, or neither.

(i) Adenine (1)
(ii) Hydrogen bonds between bases (1)
(iii) Ribose (1)
(iv) Uracil (1)
hints: Which sugar and base are unique to RNA?
questions.solution:
(i) Both [B1]
(ii) DNA only (mRNA is single-stranded) [B1]
(iii) mRNA only [B1]
(iv) mRNA only [B1]

questions.prompt: Give four differences between the structure of DNA and the structure of tRNA. (4)
questions.solution:
DNA is double-stranded; tRNA is a single strand folded into a clover shape [B1]
DNA contains deoxyribose; tRNA contains ribose [B1]
DNA contains thymine; tRNA contains uracil [B1]
tRNA has an anticodon and an amino acid binding site; DNA is much longer [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the structure of a DNA molecule. (4)
hints: How are the two strands held together?
questions.solution:
Polymer of nucleotides, each with deoxyribose, a phosphate group and a base [B1]
Sugar–phosphate backbone joined by phosphodiester bonds [B1]
Two antiparallel strands held by hydrogen bonds between complementary bases (A–T, C–G) [B1]
Twisted into a double helix [B1]

questions.prompt: Classify glucose and sucrose as monosaccharide or disaccharide. (1)
hints: Sucrose is made of two sugars.
questions.solution: Glucose: monosaccharide; sucrose: disaccharide [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the disaccharide made of glucose and galactose. (1)
questions.solution: Lactose [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the test used to show that a solution contains a reducing sugar, and the positive result. (1)
questions.solution: Benedict's test — heat; blue to brick-red precipitate [B1]

questions.prompt:
After treatment with a cancer drug, the concentrations of several polar amino acids in heart muscle proteins fell, while non-polar amino acids increased.

Analyse what this suggests about the effect of the drug on proteins in heart muscle. (6)
questions.solution:
The drug changes the proportion of amino acids in heart muscle proteins [B1]
Polar R groups form hydrogen / ionic bonds; non-polar R groups form hydrophobic interactions [B1]
So different bonds form, changing tertiary structure [B1]
Proteins may fold differently / become less soluble [B1]
Contractile proteins (actin / myosin) may not function properly [B1]
Data show correlation; mechanism not proven; need sample size / statistics [B1]
Level-marked (5–6 marks).

questions.prompt: Describe the four levels of protein structure. (6)
hints: Include the bonds at each level.
questions.solution:
Primary: sequence of amino acids joined by peptide bonds [B1]
Secondary: α-helix or β-pleated sheet held by hydrogen bonds [B1]
Tertiary: further folding into a 3D shape [B1]
Held by ionic bonds, disulfide bridges, hydrogen bonds and hydrophobic interactions [B1]
Quaternary: two or more polypeptides joined [B1]
May include prosthetic groups (e.g. haem) [B1]
Level-marked (5–6 marks).

questions.prompt: Explain how the structure of haemoglobin is related to its function. (6)
questions.solution:
Four polypeptide chains (2 α, 2 β) — quaternary structure [B1]
Each has a haem group containing Fe²⁺ that binds one O₂ [B1]
So each molecule carries four O₂ [B1]
Globular and soluble, so carried in red blood cells / in solution [B1]
Cooperative binding — binding of one O₂ changes shape, making it easier for others to bind [B1]
Hydrophilic R groups on the outside; hydrophobic inside [B1]
Level-marked (5–6 marks).

questions.prompt: Explain why a change in the amino acids in a muscle protein could weaken the muscle. (2)
questions.solution:
Different amino acids change the tertiary structure / shape of the protein [B1]
So actin and myosin can't bind / form cross-bridges effectively, reducing force of contraction [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why proteins denature at high temperatures. (2)
questions.solution:
Increased kinetic energy breaks hydrogen and ionic bonds [B1]
So tertiary structure / shape changes and the protein loses its function [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why extreme pH can stop an enzyme working. (2)
questions.solution:
H⁺ / OH⁻ ions interfere with ionic and hydrogen bonds in the enzyme [B1]
Active site changes shape, so substrate no longer fits [B1]

questions.prompt: Which bonds are found in both the secondary and tertiary structure of a protein? (1)
hints: Between N–H and C=O, or R groups.
questions.solution: Hydrogen bonds [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the amino acid whose R groups form disulfide bridges. (1)
questions.solution: Cysteine [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the bond found in primary structure. (1)
questions.solution: Peptide bond [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the reaction that breaks down glycogen into glucose. (1)
questions.solution: Hydrolysis of glycosidic bonds [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the reaction that forms a glycosidic bond. (1)
questions.solution: Condensation reaction between two monosaccharides, releasing water [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the bond that joins nucleotides in a polynucleotide. (1)
questions.solution: Phosphodiester bond [B1]

questions.prompt: State the difference between α-glucose and β-glucose. (1)
questions.solution: In α-glucose the OH on carbon 1 is below the ring; in β-glucose it is above [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the type of glucose that makes up glycogen. (1)
questions.solution: α-glucose [B1]

questions.prompt: Give the molecular formula of glucose. (1)
questions.solution: C₆H₁₂O₆ [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how the structure of glycogen is related to its function as an energy store. (3)
questions.solution:
Highly branched, so many ends for rapid hydrolysis to release glucose [B1]
Compact, so lots of energy stored in a small space [B1]
Insoluble, so doesn't affect water potential / can't leave cells [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how the structure of cellulose makes it suitable for plant cell walls. (3)
questions.solution:
β-glucose joined by 1,4 glycosidic bonds with alternate molecules inverted, giving straight chains [B1]
Many hydrogen bonds between parallel chains form microfibrils [B1]
Gives high tensile strength to resist turgor pressure [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how the structure of starch makes it a suitable storage molecule in plants. (3)
questions.solution:
Amylose coils into a compact helix [B1]
Amylopectin is branched so glucose can be released quickly [B1]
Insoluble, so no osmotic effect [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the three components of a phospholipid. (1)
questions.solution: Glycerol, two fatty acids and a phosphate group [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the bond between glycerol and a fatty acid. (1)
questions.solution: Ester bond [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between a saturated and an unsaturated fatty acid. (1)
questions.solution: Saturated has no C=C double bonds; unsaturated has one or more C=C double bonds [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the structure of a phospholipid. (2)
questions.solution:
Glycerol joined to two fatty acids (ester bonds) and a phosphate group [B1]
Hydrophilic phosphate head and two hydrophobic fatty acid tails [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the emulsion test for lipids. (2)
questions.solution:
Shake the sample with ethanol, then add water [B1]
A white / milky emulsion shows lipid is present [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why phospholipids form a bilayer in water. (2)
questions.solution:
Hydrophilic heads are attracted to water and face outwards [B1]
Hydrophobic tails are repelled by water and face inwards, away from water on either side [B1]

questions.prompt:
(i) Name the monomer of cellulose. (1)
(ii) Name the product of complete hydrolysis of cellulose and the type of bond broken. (2)
questions.solution:
(i) β-glucose [B1]
(ii) β-glucose [B1]
1,4 glycosidic bonds are broken by hydrolysis [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why elephants rely on microorganisms in their gut to digest cellulose. (3)
questions.solution:
Cellulose is broken down by the enzyme cellulase [B1]
Mammals do not produce cellulase [B1]
Gut microorganisms produce cellulase and hydrolyse cellulose into glucose / fatty acids the elephant can use [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the test for starch and explain why cellulose does not give a positive result. (3)
questions.solution:
Add iodine solution; blue-black colour shows starch [B1]
Iodine fits inside the amylose helix [B1]
Cellulose has straight chains, not a helix, so no colour change [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how the structure of cellulose is adapted to its function in plant cell walls. (3)
questions.solution:
β-glucose with alternate monomers inverted forms long, straight, unbranched chains [B1]
Parallel chains linked by many hydrogen bonds to form microfibrils and fibres [B1]
High tensile strength prevents cells bursting when turgid [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why paper made from plant fibres is strong but becomes weak when wet. (3)
questions.solution:
Cellulose fibres are held together by many hydrogen bonds [B1]
Water molecules form hydrogen bonds with cellulose [B1]
Disrupting the hydrogen bonds between fibres, so they separate [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why cellulose is insoluble and hard to digest, while starch is easily digested by humans. (3)
questions.solution:
Cellulose has β-1,4 bonds; starch has α-1,4 and 1,6 bonds [B1]
Human amylase is specific to α-glycosidic bonds [B1]
Cellulose chains packed in microfibrils with many hydrogen bonds, so enzymes can't access them easily [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the folds of the inner membrane of a mitochondrion. (1)
questions.solution: Cristae [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the fluid inside a chloroplast, where the Calvin cycle occurs. (1)
questions.solution: Stroma [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the fluid-filled region inside a mitochondrion where the Krebs cycle occurs. (1)
questions.solution: Matrix [B1]

questions.prompt:
One micrograph of a mitochondrion was taken with a transmission electron microscope (TEM) and one with a scanning electron microscope (SEM).

Explain why they look different. (2)
hints: TEM passes electrons through the specimen.
SEM bounces electrons off the surface.
questions.solution:
TEM shows a 2D image of internal structure (thin section) [B1]
SEM shows a 3D image of the surface only [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why an electron microscope has a higher resolution than a light microscope. (2)
hints: Resolution = ability to distinguish two points.
questions.solution:
Electrons have a much shorter wavelength than light [B1]
So two points closer together can be distinguished [B1]

questions.prompt: Give two advantages of light microscopes over electron microscopes. (2)
questions.solution:
Living specimens can be viewed [B1]
Natural colour / cheaper / portable / simpler preparation / no artefacts from vacuum [B1]

questions.prompt:
The inner membrane of a mitochondrion has a protein:lipid ratio of 3 : 2, while the outer membrane has a ratio of 1 : 1.

Explain this difference. (6)
hints: What processes happen on the inner membrane?
questions.solution:
Inner membrane is the site of oxidative phosphorylation [B1]
Contains many electron carrier proteins of the electron transport chain [B1]
Contains ATP synthase enzymes [B1]
Contains transport proteins for ADP, ATP, pyruvate [B1]
Inner membrane impermeable to H⁺, maintaining a proton gradient [B1]
Outer membrane has fewer functions, mainly a barrier with channel proteins [B1]
Level-marked (5–6 marks).

questions.prompt: Explain how the structure of a chloroplast is adapted for photosynthesis. (6)
questions.solution:
Thylakoid membranes stacked into grana give a large surface area [B1]
For photosystems / chlorophyll to absorb light [B1]
Thylakoid membranes contain electron carriers and ATP synthase [B1]
Stroma contains enzymes (RuBisCO) for the Calvin cycle [B1]
Starch grains store products; own DNA and ribosomes to make proteins [B1]
Small space inside thylakoids allows H⁺ gradient to build up [B1]
Level-marked (5–6 marks).

questions.prompt: Describe the different roles of proteins in cell surface membranes. (6)
questions.solution:
Channel proteins allow ions / polar molecules to diffuse through [B1]
Carrier proteins for facilitated diffusion and active transport [B1]
Receptor proteins bind hormones / neurotransmitters [B1]
Glycoproteins act as antigens for cell recognition [B1]
Enzymes, e.g. in the microvilli of the small intestine [B1]
Anchoring the cytoskeleton / cell adhesion [B1]
Level-marked (5–6 marks).

questions.prompt: State what is meant by DNA methylation. (1)
questions.solution: Addition of methyl groups to DNA (cytosine bases), usually switching genes off [B1]

questions.prompt: State what is meant by histone acetylation. (1)
questions.solution: Addition of acetyl groups to histones, loosening chromatin so genes can be transcribed [B1]

questions.prompt: Give the meaning of the term epigenetics. (1)
hints: Heritable but not the base sequence.
questions.solution: Heritable changes in gene expression that do not involve changes to the base sequence of DNA [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the differences between totipotent, pluripotent and multipotent stem cells. (3)
hints: How many cell types can each form?
questions.solution:
Totipotent cells can form any cell type, including placenta (zygote / early morula) [B1]
Pluripotent cells can form any body cell type but not placenta (inner cell mass of blastocyst) [B1]
Multipotent cells form only a limited range of related cells (adult stem cells, e.g. bone marrow) [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the development of a human embryo from a zygote to a blastocyst. (3)
questions.solution:
Zygote divides by mitosis (cleavage) to form a ball of cells — morula [B1]
Cells continue dividing and fluid fills a cavity, forming a blastocyst [B1]
Blastocyst has an outer layer (trophoblast) and an inner cell mass of pluripotent cells [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why stem cells from an early embryo are more useful for research than adult stem cells, and give one ethical objection. (3)
questions.solution:
Embryonic cells are totipotent / pluripotent, so can form more cell types [B1]
Adult stem cells are multipotent / harder to find and grow [B1]
Objection: embryo is destroyed — some believe it has the right to life [B1]

questions.prompt:
DNA methylation is low in the early embryo and rises as cells become specialised.

Explain why DNA methylation is involved in embryo development. (2)
hints: Specialised cells use only some genes.
questions.solution:
Low methylation early means most genes can be expressed, so cells are totipotent / pluripotent [B1]
Increased methylation switches off genes not needed, so cells differentiate / specialise [B1]

questions.prompt: Identical twins have the same DNA but can develop different diseases later in life. Suggest why. (2)
questions.solution:
Different environments / lifestyles cause different epigenetic changes (methylation / histone modification) [B1]
So different genes are switched on or off, giving different phenotypes [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how methylation of a gene's promoter region prevents the gene from being expressed. (2)
questions.solution:
Methyl groups prevent transcription factors / RNA polymerase binding to the promoter [B1]
So the gene is not transcribed / no mRNA made [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why some cells cannot differentiate into other cell types. (2)
questions.solution:
Genes needed for other cell types have been permanently switched off (e.g. by methylation) [B1]
Some cells have lost their nucleus or other organelles (e.g. red blood cells, xylem) [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why all the cells in a person contain the same genes but have different structures. (2)
questions.solution:
Different genes are expressed / switched on in different cells [B1]
So different proteins are made, giving different structures and functions [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why plant cuttings can grow into whole new plants. (2)
questions.solution:
Plants retain meristem cells that are totipotent / can differentiate into any cell type [B1]
So the cutting can form roots and other tissues [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the virus that contains RNA and the enzyme reverse transcriptase. (1)
questions.solution: HIV [B1]

questions.prompt: Name a virus that infects bacteria and contains DNA. (1)
questions.solution: λ (lambda) phage [B1]

questions.prompt: Give one feature that all viruses have in common. (1)
questions.solution: Nucleic acid (DNA or RNA) surrounded by a protein coat (capsid) [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the lytic cycle of a virus. (2)
hints: Viral genes are expressed straight away.
questions.solution:
Viral nucleic acid is replicated and viral proteins made using the host cell's machinery [B1]
New virus particles assemble and the cell bursts (lysis), releasing them [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how a virus attaches to and enters a host cell. (2)
questions.solution:
Attachment proteins on the virus bind to complementary receptors on the host cell membrane [B1]
Viral nucleic acid is injected / virus enters by endocytosis or membrane fusion [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why viruses can only infect certain types of cells. (2)
questions.solution:
Viral attachment proteins only bind to specific complementary receptors [B1]
Only cells with those receptors can be infected (e.g. HIV binds CD4 on T helper cells) [B1]

questions.prompt: State what is meant by latency in viral infections. (2)
questions.solution:
Viral nucleic acid is inserted into the host DNA / stays in the cell [B1]
But is not expressed, so no new viruses are made for a time; it can later become active [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why latent viruses are difficult for the immune system to destroy. (2)
questions.solution:
No viral proteins / antigens are produced, so infected cells are not recognised [B1]
T killer cells can't identify and destroy them [B1]

questions.prompt: Give an example of a virus that shows latency and explain why symptoms can recur. (2)
questions.solution:
e.g. herpes simplex (cold sores) / varicella zoster (chickenpox → shingles) [B1]
Virus stays latent in nerve cells and can be reactivated (e.g. by stress), entering the lytic cycle [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how meiosis produces genetic variation in gametes. (2)
questions.solution:
Crossing over between homologous chromosomes swaps sections of chromatids, producing new allele combinations [B1]
Independent assortment — homologous pairs line up randomly at metaphase I [B1]

questions.prompt: An organism has a diploid number of 8. Calculate how many different combinations of chromosomes are possible in its gametes from independent assortment alone. (2)
questions.solution:
Haploid number = 4 [M1]
2⁴ = 16 combinations [A1]

questions.prompt: Give two differences between mitosis and meiosis. (2)
questions.solution:
Meiosis has two divisions, producing four cells; mitosis has one, producing two [B1]
Meiosis produces haploid, genetically different cells; mitosis produces diploid, identical cells [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how fertilisation in humans forms a zygote. (3)
questions.solution:
Acrosome releases enzymes that digest the zona pellucida [B1]
Sperm and egg membranes fuse; cortical reaction hardens the zona pellucida, preventing other sperm entering [B1]
Sperm nucleus enters; haploid nuclei fuse to form a diploid zygote [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe double fertilisation in flowering plants. (3)
hints: Pollen tube with two male nuclei.
One fuses with the egg, one with the polar nuclei.
questions.solution:
Pollen tube grows down the style, carrying two male nuclei into the ovule [B1]
One male nucleus fuses with the egg cell to form a diploid zygote [B1]
The other fuses with two polar nuclei to form a triploid endosperm nucleus [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain the importance of meiosis and fertilisation in sexual reproduction. (3)
questions.solution:
Meiosis halves the chromosome number so gametes are haploid [B1]
Fertilisation restores the diploid number [B1]
Both create genetic variation (crossing over, independent assortment, random fertilisation) [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the λ (lambda) phage. (1)
questions.solution: A DNA virus with a complex capsid (head and tail) that infects bacteria [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe tobacco mosaic virus (TMV). (1)
questions.solution: An RNA virus with a helical capsid, infecting plants [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the structure of HIV. (1)
questions.solution: RNA retrovirus with a lipid envelope, a protein capsid and reverse transcriptase [B1]

questions.prompt:
Most Archaea have membranes made of a single layer of bipolar lipids, which have a hydrophilic group at each end joined by a long hydrophobic chain.

Explain why these lipids form a monolayer membrane. (2)
questions.solution:
Each end is hydrophilic, so faces the water on one side of the membrane [B1]
The hydrophobic middle spans the membrane, so a single layer forms a stable barrier [B1]

questions.prompt: Give two differences between Archaea and Bacteria. (2)
questions.solution:
Archaea have different membrane lipids (ether-linked, branched) [B1]
Archaea lack peptidoglycan in cell walls / have histones / RNA polymerase more like eukaryotes [B1]

questions.prompt: Give two pieces of evidence that led to the three-domain system. (2)
questions.solution:
Differences in base sequences of ribosomal RNA [B1]
Differences in membrane lipids / RNA polymerase / cell wall composition [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why the lipid composition of prokaryotic membranes must change when the temperature changes. (3)
questions.solution:
At high temperatures membranes become too fluid / too permeable, so substances leak [B1]
At low temperatures membranes become too rigid, so transport proteins can't work / cells can't divide [B1]
Changing fatty acids (saturation / branching / chain length) keeps fluidity constant [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how cholesterol affects the fluidity of animal cell membranes. (3)
questions.solution:
Cholesterol fits between phospholipids [B1]
At high temperatures it restricts phospholipid movement, reducing fluidity [B1]
At low temperatures it prevents phospholipids packing closely, keeping the membrane fluid [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why plants living in cold climates have more unsaturated fatty acids in their membranes. (3)
questions.solution:
C=C double bonds produce kinks in fatty acid tails [B1]
So phospholipids can't pack closely together [B1]
Membrane stays fluid at low temperatures [B1]

questions.prompt: Radioactive amino acids were given to a cell. Give the sequence of organelles in which radioactivity appears, and explain why. (2)
questions.solution:
Rough ER → Golgi apparatus → secretory vesicles / cell membrane [B1]
Proteins are made on ribosomes on the rough ER, then modified in the Golgi and packaged into vesicles [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the organelle that makes lipids and steroids, and the organelle that produces ribosomes. (2)
questions.solution:
Smooth endoplasmic reticulum [B1]
Nucleolus [B1]

questions.prompt: Give the function of centrioles in animal cells. (2)
questions.solution:
Form the spindle fibres during cell division [B1]
Spindle separates chromosomes / chromatids [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain one function of lysosomes. (2)
questions.solution:
Contain digestive (hydrolytic) enzymes [B1]
e.g. fuse with phagosomes to digest pathogens / break down worn-out organelles (autolysis) [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain one function of the Golgi apparatus. (2)
questions.solution:
Modifies proteins, e.g. adding carbohydrates to make glycoproteins [B1]
Packages them into vesicles for secretion / makes lysosomes [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain the function of the nuclear pores. (2)
questions.solution:
Allow mRNA (and ribosome subunits) to leave the nucleus [B1]
Allow proteins such as transcription factors / nucleotides to enter [B1]

questions.prompt:
From day 0 to day 6 of human embryo development, the nucleus-to-cytoplasm ratio increases in all cells, increasing more in inner cell mass cells than in trophectoderm cells.

Comment on these changes. (3)
questions.solution:
During cleavage, cells divide by mitosis without growing, so the cytoplasm volume per cell decreases [B1]
Nucleus size stays about the same, so the ratio increases [B1]
Inner cell mass cells divide more / are smaller, as they form the embryo itself [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the roles of the inner cell mass and the trophoblast of a blastocyst. (3)
questions.solution:
Inner cell mass develops into the embryo — pluripotent cells [B1]
Trophoblast forms the outer layer and develops into the placenta [B1]
Trophoblast helps implantation into the uterus wall [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the main events of the cell cycle. (3)
questions.solution:
G1: cell grows and makes organelles and proteins [B1]
S phase: DNA replicates; G2: further growth and checks [B1]
Mitosis divides the nucleus, then cytokinesis divides the cytoplasm [B1]

questions.prompt:
A survey counted 20 birds of species A, 10 of species B and 5 of species C.

Calculate the index of diversity, D = N(N − 1) ÷ Σn(n − 1). (3)

In a pond, 12 individuals each of species P, Q and R were found.

Calculate D = N(N − 1) ÷ Σn(n − 1). (3)

Two meadows each contain 3 species and 30 plants. Meadow 1: 10, 10, 10. Meadow 2: 26, 2, 2.

Calculate D for each and state which is more diverse. (3)
questions.solution:
N(N − 1) = 870; Meadow 1: Σ = 3 × 90 = 270, D = 3.22 [M1]
Meadow 2: Σ = 650 + 2 + 2 = 654, D = 1.33 [M1]
Meadow 1 is more diverse (more even distribution) [A1]

questions.prompt: Explain why an index of diversity is a better measure of biodiversity than species richness alone. (2)
hints: What else does the index include?
questions.solution:
Index takes into account the number of individuals of each species (evenness) as well as the number of species [B1]
A community dominated by one species is less diverse, even with the same number of species [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why genetic diversity is important for the survival of a species. (2)
questions.solution:
More alleles / variation in the population [B1]
More likely some individuals survive environmental change or disease, so the species can adapt [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how biodiversity in a woodland could be compared before and after logging. (2)
questions.solution:
Use quadrats / traps placed randomly in the same area before and after [B1]
Count species and individuals and calculate an index of diversity for each [B1]

questions.prompt:
The brown tree snake was accidentally introduced to the island of Guam. Over five years, the number of native bird species fell from 12 to 3, and the index of diversity fell from 8.5 to 1.4.

Comment on the effect of the snake on bird species. (4)
questions.solution:
Bird species richness fell by 75 % and diversity fell sharply [B1]
Snake preyed on birds and eggs; birds had no adaptations to avoid it [B1]
Snake had no natural predators on the island, so its population grew [B1]
Data show correlation; other factors may have contributed [B1]

questions.prompt: Grey squirrels were introduced to Britain and the native red squirrel population has declined. Suggest reasons for the decline. (4)
questions.solution:
Greys compete for the same food (nuts / seeds) and habitat [B1]
Greys are larger / better at digesting acorns [B1]
Greys carry squirrelpox virus, which kills reds but not greys [B1]
Habitat loss also reduces red populations [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why invasive species often reduce biodiversity. (4)
questions.solution:
No natural predators / diseases in the new habitat, so populations grow rapidly [B1]
Outcompete native species for food / space [B1]
Prey on native species that have no defences [B1]
Introduce new diseases; can cause extinctions [B1]

questions.prompt: After birds declined on Guam, plant biodiversity also fell. Give two reasons why. (2)
hints: What do birds do for plants?
questions.solution:
Fewer birds to disperse seeds [B1]
Fewer birds to pollinate flowers / control insect pests [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why removing a top predator can reduce the biodiversity of an ecosystem. (2)
questions.solution:
Herbivore / prey populations increase [B1]
Overgrazing / one prey species outcompetes others, reducing species numbers [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain what is meant by a keystone species, with an example. (2)
questions.solution:
A species with a disproportionately large effect on its ecosystem; its removal changes the community greatly [B1]
e.g. sea otters eat sea urchins, protecting kelp forests [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how seed banks are used to conserve plant biodiversity. (4)
questions.solution:
Seeds are collected from many plants of each species to maximise genetic diversity [B1]
Seeds are dried and stored at low temperature (about −20 °C) [B1]
Viability is tested regularly by germinating samples [B1]
Seeds can be grown to reintroduce plants into the wild / used for research [B1]

questions.prompt: Compare in situ and ex situ conservation, giving an example of each. (4)
questions.solution:
In situ: conservation in the natural habitat, e.g. national parks / marine reserves [B1]
Protects whole ecosystem and species interactions [B1]
Ex situ: outside the natural habitat, e.g. zoos, botanic gardens, seed banks [B1]
Protects species under severe threat, but small populations / reduced genetic diversity / adapting to captivity [B1]

questions.prompt: Give advantages and disadvantages of seed banks compared with conserving plants in their natural habitat. (4)
questions.solution:
Advantage: large numbers stored in a small space, cheaply, for a long time [B1]
Advantage: protected from disease, habitat loss, climate change [B1]
Disadvantage: some seeds (recalcitrant) can't be dried / frozen [B1]
Disadvantage: stored seeds don't evolve with the environment; ecosystem not protected [B1]

questions.prompt: The malaria pathogen is Plasmodium falciparum. Name the genus and the kingdom it belongs to. (1)
hints: The genus is the first word.
questions.solution: Genus Plasmodium; kingdom Protoctista [B1]

questions.prompt: Give the order of taxonomic ranks from domain to species. (1)
questions.solution: Domain, kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the three domains in the three-domain classification system. (1)
questions.solution: Bacteria, Archaea, Eukarya [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why an index of diversity is a better measure of biodiversity than counting the number of species. (1)
questions.solution: It takes into account the number of individuals of each species as well as the number of species [B1]

questions.prompt: Give one reason why it is hard to measure biodiversity accurately. (1)
questions.solution: Can't count every organism; some species are rare / hidden / mobile, so samples may not be representative [B1]

questions.prompt: Name a technique used to sample flying insects. (1)
questions.solution: Sweep net / light trap / Malaise trap [B1]

questions.prompt: Give two advantages of in situ conservation of elephants compared with ex situ conservation. (2)
questions.solution:
Elephants stay in their natural habitat, so natural behaviour and interactions continue [B1]
Whole ecosystem and other species are protected / larger populations, more genetic diversity [B1]

questions.prompt: Give two advantages of ex situ conservation. (2)
questions.solution:
Protects animals from poaching, predators and habitat loss [B1]
Captive breeding to increase numbers / research / education [B1]

questions.prompt: Give two problems with reintroducing animals bred in zoos to the wild. (2)
questions.solution:
Animals may lack survival skills (hunting, avoiding predators) [B1]
Habitat may be lost / disease brought into wild populations / low genetic diversity [B1]

questions.prompt:
In an area where local people make paper from elephant dung, the index of diversity rose from 2.8 to 3.6 over two years. In a protected area where local people were banned, it fell from 2.4 to 2.2.

Explain the effect of the paper project on biodiversity. (4)
hints: Why would local people protect elephants?
questions.solution:
Diversity rose by 29 % with the project but fell by 8 % in the banned area [B1]
Local people earn money from elephants, so have an incentive to protect them / less poaching [B1]
Elephants disperse seeds and create habitats, increasing biodiversity [B1]
Banning people may cause resentment, poaching or illegal activity; only two areas / two years [B1]

questions.prompt: Discuss the benefits and drawbacks of ecotourism for conservation. (4)
questions.solution:
Provides income for conservation and local communities [B1]
Raises awareness [B1]
Visitors may disturb wildlife / damage habitats [B1]
Travel causes pollution / CO₂; money may not reach local people [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why involving local communities is important for successful conservation. (4)
questions.solution:
Local people use the land and resources, so their cooperation is needed [B1]
If they benefit (income, jobs), they are less likely to poach or clear land [B1]
Local knowledge helps monitoring [B1]
Reduces conflict between people and wildlife [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe two limitations of CITES in conserving species such as elephants. (2)
questions.solution:
Difficult to enforce / illegal trade and poaching continue [B1]
Only controls international trade — does not protect habitats; not all countries are members [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe what CITES does. (2)
questions.solution:
International agreement that regulates trade in endangered species and their products [B1]
Bans trade in the most endangered species (e.g. ivory); requires permits for others [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the aims of the Rio Convention on Biological Diversity. (2)
questions.solution:
Conservation of biodiversity and sustainable use of resources [B1]
Fair sharing of benefits from genetic resources; countries make national strategies [B1]

questions.prompt:
Lipoproteins have an outer layer of phospholipids and proteins surrounding a core of cholesterol and triglycerides.

Explain how this structure allows lipids to be transported in the blood. (3)
questions.solution:
Lipids are insoluble / non-polar, so cannot dissolve in plasma [B1]
Hydrophilic phosphate heads and proteins face outwards towards water [B1]
Hydrophobic tails face inwards, surrounding the lipid core, so the complex is soluble [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the structure of a triglyceride and explain why it is a good energy store. (3)
questions.solution:
One glycerol joined to three fatty acids by ester bonds (condensation) [B1]
Many C–H bonds release a lot of energy when oxidised [B1]
Insoluble, so doesn't affect water potential [B1]

questions.prompt: Compare the structure of a triglyceride and a phospholipid. (3)
questions.solution:
Both contain glycerol and fatty acids joined by ester bonds [B1]
Triglyceride has three fatty acids; phospholipid has two and a phosphate group [B1]
Phospholipid has a hydrophilic head; triglyceride is entirely hydrophobic [B1]

questions.prompt: HDLs are about 50 % protein and LDLs about 20 % protein. Explain why LDLs have a lower density than HDLs. (2)
questions.solution:
Protein is denser than lipid [B1]
LDLs have a lower proportion of protein / higher proportion of lipid, so are less dense [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why a high ratio of HDL to LDL is associated with a lower risk of heart disease. (2)
questions.solution:
HDLs transport cholesterol from tissues to the liver for removal [B1]
So less cholesterol deposited in artery walls / less atheroma [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how statins reduce the risk of cardiovascular disease. (2)
questions.solution:
Statins inhibit an enzyme in the liver that makes cholesterol [B1]
So less LDL cholesterol in the blood, less atheroma formation [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why raised levels of LDL in the blood may increase the risk of heart disease. (4)
questions.solution:
LDL deposits cholesterol in the walls of arteries (where endothelium is damaged) [B1]
Forming atheroma / plaque, narrowing the lumen [B1]
Less blood / oxygen reaches heart muscle via the coronary arteries [B1]
Plaque may rupture, causing a clot that blocks a coronary artery, so heart muscle dies (myocardial infarction) [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how smoking increases the risk of cardiovascular disease. (4)
questions.solution:
Chemicals in smoke damage the endothelium, starting atheroma formation [B1]
Nicotine raises heart rate / blood pressure / makes platelets sticky [B1]
Carbon monoxide binds to haemoglobin, reducing oxygen transport [B1]
So heart must work harder; increased risk of clots and heart attack [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how an aneurysm can develop in an artery affected by atherosclerosis. (4)
questions.solution:
Atheroma narrows the lumen, increasing blood pressure [B1]
Artery wall is damaged / loses elasticity [B1]
Wall weakens and bulges under pressure (aneurysm) [B1]
Aneurysm may burst, causing haemorrhage [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how guard cells open a stoma. (3)
questions.solution:
H⁺ ions are actively pumped out of guard cells, using ATP; K⁺ ions diffuse in [B1]
Starch converted to malate; water potential of guard cells falls [B1]
Water enters by osmosis; cells become turgid and bend (thicker inner wall), opening the stoma [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how abscisic acid (ABA) causes stomata to close in dry conditions. (3)
questions.solution:
ABA binds to receptors on guard cells [B1]
K⁺ ions leave the guard cells / Ca²⁺ enters; water potential rises [B1]
Water leaves by osmosis, guard cells become flaccid and the stoma closes [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain the factors that increase the rate of transpiration. (3)
questions.solution:
Higher temperature increases evaporation and diffusion [B1]
Lower humidity / wind increases the water potential gradient [B1]
Higher light intensity opens more stomata [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how weakened cardiac muscle could affect a person. (3)
questions.solution:
Weaker contraction reduces stroke volume / cardiac output [B1]
Less oxygen and glucose delivered to tissues, so less aerobic respiration [B1]
Person becomes tired / breathless; fluid may build up (heart failure) [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain the effect of a blocked coronary artery on the heart. (3)
hints: Coronary arteries supply the heart muscle.
questions.solution:
Less blood / oxygen reaches part of the heart muscle [B1]
Muscle cells can't respire aerobically, so they die [B1]
Heart attack / myocardial infarction; heart can't pump effectively [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how the heart's own blood supply is adapted to its high demand for oxygen. (3)
questions.solution:
Coronary arteries branch from the aorta, supplying blood at high pressure [B1]
Dense network of capillaries in cardiac muscle [B1]
Short diffusion distance to many mitochondria for aerobic respiration [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the type of bond responsible for cohesion between water molecules. (1)
hints: Between δ+ H and δ− O.
questions.solution: Hydrogen bonds [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why water is a good solvent. (1)
questions.solution: Water is polar, so it attracts and surrounds ions and other polar molecules [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why water's high specific heat capacity is important to organisms. (1)
questions.solution: Lots of energy needed to change its temperature, so aquatic habitats and body temperature stay stable [B1]

questions.prompt:
The Carrico index is the partial pressure of oxygen in arterial blood divided by the proportion of oxygen in inspired air. A baby had a Carrico index of 60 kPa while breathing air (0.21 oxygen).

Calculate the partial pressure of oxygen in the baby's arterial blood. (1)
A patient on 40 % oxygen has an arterial oxygen partial pressure of 16 kPa. Calculate the Carrico index (pO₂ ÷ oxygen fraction). (1)
Air contains 21 % oxygen. Calculate the partial pressure of oxygen in air at an atmospheric pressure of 101 kPa. (1)

In acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), alveoli produce too little surfactant and cannot expand properly.

Explain why babies with ARDS have a lower partial pressure of oxygen in their blood. (4)
questions.solution:
Without surfactant, surface tension of water lining the alveoli is high, so alveoli collapse / can't inflate [B1]
Smaller surface area for gas exchange [B1]
Fluid in alveoli increases diffusion distance [B1]
Less oxygen diffuses into the blood [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how the alveoli are adapted for efficient gas exchange. (4)
questions.solution:
Very large surface area (millions of alveoli) [B1]
Thin walls — one cell thick (squamous epithelium) — short diffusion distance [B1]
Good blood supply / capillary network maintains a steep concentration gradient [B1]
Ventilation replaces air, maintaining the gradient; surfactant prevents collapse [B1]

questions.prompt: Use Fick's law to explain why emphysema reduces the rate of gas exchange. (4)
questions.solution:
Fick's law: rate ∝ surface area × concentration difference ÷ diffusion distance [B1]
Alveolar walls break down, so surface area falls [B1]
Loss of elastic tissue means less air is exhaled, so concentration gradient is reduced [B1]
So less oxygen diffuses into the blood [B1]

questions.prompt:
The partial pressure of oxygen is 5.3 kPa in pulmonary arterial blood and 13.3 kPa in other arterial blood.

Calculate the ratio to one decimal place. (1)
The pO₂ in alveolar air is 13.5 kPa and in muscle tissue during exercise is 2.7 kPa. Calculate the ratio. (1)
Haemoglobin is 98 % saturated in the lungs and 25 % saturated in active muscle. What percentage of the oxygen carried is released to the muscle? (1)
Explain why the partial pressure of oxygen is lower in the pulmonary artery than in other arteries. (2)
hints: Where has pulmonary arterial blood come from?
questions.solution:
Pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood from the body (via the right ventricle) to the lungs [B1]
Oxygen has been released to respiring tissues; other arteries carry blood just oxygenated in the lungs [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how the Bohr effect helps release oxygen to respiring muscles. (2)
questions.solution:
Respiring muscles produce CO₂, which lowers pH [B1]
Haemoglobin's affinity for O₂ decreases (curve shifts right), so more O₂ is unloaded [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why fetal haemoglobin has a higher affinity for oxygen than adult haemoglobin. (2)
hints: Where does the fetus get oxygen?
questions.solution:
Fetus gets oxygen from mother's blood in the placenta, where pO₂ is low [B1]
Higher affinity allows fetal haemoglobin to take up oxygen from maternal haemoglobin [B1]

questions.prompt:
(i) Describe the net movement of oxygen and carbon dioxide in a plant root. (1)
(ii) Name the gas exchange openings in the bark of a woody stem. (1)
hints: Roots respire but do not photosynthesise.
questions.solution:
(i) Oxygen diffuses in; carbon dioxide diffuses out [B1]
(ii) Lenticels [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain the net gas exchange of a leaf in bright light and in the dark. (2)
questions.solution:
In bright light, photosynthesis is faster than respiration: net CO₂ uptake and O₂ release [B1]
In the dark, only respiration: O₂ uptake and CO₂ release [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how the structure of a leaf is adapted for gas exchange. (2)
questions.solution:
Many stomata allow gases in and out [B1]
Air spaces in the spongy mesophyll; thin leaves give short diffusion paths and a large surface area [B1]

questions.prompt:
Insects lost 0.10 mg of water per hour in air at 0 % humidity and 0.07 mg per hour at 80 % humidity.

(i) Calculate the percentage increase in water loss at 0 % humidity, to 2 decimal places. (1)
(ii) Explain the result. (3)
questions.solution:
(i) 42.86 % [B1]
(ii) At 0 % humidity there is a steeper water potential / concentration gradient from tracheae to air [B1]
Water vapour diffuses out of the spiracles faster [B1]
Insects can close spiracles to reduce loss, but must open them for gas exchange [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how gas exchange takes place in insects. (4)
questions.solution:
Air enters through spiracles [B1]
Passes along tracheae to tracheoles [B1]
Tracheoles reach individual cells, so oxygen diffuses directly into cells [B1]
Ventilation by abdominal pumping; fluid at tracheole ends withdrawn during activity [B1]

questions.prompt: Insects kept in air with high CO₂ opened their spiracles more and lost more water. Explain why. (4)
questions.solution:
High CO₂ in the tracheae stimulates the spiracles to open [B1]
To allow CO₂ to diffuse out / more O₂ in [B1]
Open spiracles allow more water vapour to diffuse out [B1]
Shows a trade-off between gas exchange and water conservation [B1]

questions.prompt:
A fish has 6480 gill filaments, each 25 mm long with 24 lamellae per mm on each side.

Calculate the total number of lamellae in standard form. (1)
Express 0.000 045 m in µm and in standard form (m). (1)
A fish has gill surface area of 0.12 m² and a mass of 0.4 kg. Calculate the gill surface area per kg. (1)
questions.solution: 0.3 m² kg⁻¹ [B1]

questions.prompt:
Data from five fish species show that the most active species (e.g. tuna) have the largest gill surface area per kg of body mass and the thinnest water–blood barrier, while slow-moving bottom-dwelling fish have small gill areas and thick barriers.

Explain the relationship between activity and gill structure. (6)
questions.solution:
Active fish respire more, so need more oxygen [B1]
Larger gill surface area allows more oxygen to diffuse into the blood [B1]
Thinner barrier gives a shorter diffusion distance [B1]
More lamellae / filaments increase surface area [B1]
Countercurrent flow maintains a concentration gradient along the whole lamella [B1]
Tuna use ram ventilation; inactive fish need less O₂ so smaller gills suffice [B1]
Level-marked (5–6 marks).

questions.prompt: Explain how the countercurrent system in fish gills maximises oxygen uptake. (6)
questions.solution:
Blood flows through lamellae in the opposite direction to water [B1]
Blood always meets water with a higher oxygen concentration [B1]
A diffusion gradient is maintained along the whole length of the lamella [B1]
So oxygen diffuses into the blood all the way along [B1]
About 80 % of oxygen can be extracted [B1]
With parallel flow, equilibrium would be reached at about 50 % [B1]
Level-marked (5–6 marks).

questions.prompt: Compare gas exchange in fish, insects and mammals. (6)
questions.solution:
All have large surface areas, thin surfaces and maintain concentration gradients [B1]
Fish: gills with lamellae; countercurrent flow; water ventilated over gills [B1]
Insects: tracheal system; air delivered directly to cells; no blood transport of gases [B1]
Mammals: alveoli with capillaries; tidal ventilation [B1]
Fish and mammals use blood (haemoglobin) to transport oxygen [B1]
Insects limit water loss via spiracles; mammals' lungs are internal to reduce water loss [B1]
Level-marked (5–6 marks).

questions.prompt:
When the left atrioventricular valve closes, the pressure difference across it is 16 kPa. The valve area is 3.5 cm².

Calculate the force on the valve, using pressure (kPa) = force (N) ÷ area (m²), with pressure converted to Pa. (3)
Describe the pressure changes in the left ventricle during one cardiac cycle and when the valves open and close. (3)
questions.solution:
Ventricular pressure rises when it contracts; AV valve closes when it exceeds atrial pressure [B1]
Semilunar valve opens when ventricular pressure exceeds aortic pressure [B1]
As ventricle relaxes, pressure falls; semilunar valve closes, then AV valve opens when below atrial pressure [B1]

questions.prompt: One cardiac cycle takes 0.8 s. Calculate the heart rate and the cardiac output if stroke volume is 80 cm³. (3)
questions.solution:
Heart rate = 60 ÷ 0.8 = 75 bpm [M1]
Cardiac output = 75 × 80 [M1]
= 6000 cm³ min⁻¹ (6 dm³ min⁻¹) [A1]

questions.prompt: Explain why people with a leaking atrioventricular valve find exercise difficult. (4)
hints: Where does blood go when the ventricle contracts?
questions.solution:
Some blood flows back into the atrium when the ventricle contracts [B1]
So less blood leaves through the aorta / stroke volume and cardiac output fall [B1]
Less oxygen delivered to muscles [B1]
More anaerobic respiration, lactate builds up, causing fatigue / breathlessness [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why a narrowed (stenosed) aortic valve makes the left ventricle wall thicken over time. (4)
questions.solution:
A narrow valve increases resistance to blood leaving the ventricle [B1]
Ventricle must generate higher pressure to pump blood out [B1]
Cardiac muscle works harder [B1]
So the muscle grows thicker (hypertrophy) [B1]

questions.prompt: A hole between the left and right ventricles allows blood to mix. Explain the effects on the body. (4)
questions.solution:
Oxygenated and deoxygenated blood mix [B1]
Blood pumped to the body has less oxygen [B1]
Less oxygen for respiration, so tiredness / breathlessness / cyanosis [B1]
Heart must work harder, increasing heart rate [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how tissue fluid is returned to the capillaries. (3)
hints: Hydrostatic pressure falls along the capillary.
Plasma proteins stay in the blood.
questions.solution:
At the venous end, hydrostatic pressure in the capillary is lower [B1]
Plasma proteins remain in the blood, so its water potential is lower than tissue fluid (oncotic pressure) [B1]
Water moves back into the capillary by osmosis; excess tissue fluid drains into lymph vessels [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how tissue fluid is formed at the arterial end of a capillary. (3)
questions.solution:
Hydrostatic pressure is high at the arterial end (from heart contraction) [B1]
This is greater than the oncotic pressure from plasma proteins [B1]
So water and small solutes (glucose, ions, oxygen) are forced out; cells and large proteins stay in [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why a diet very low in protein can lead to swelling of tissues (oedema). (3)
questions.solution:
Fewer plasma proteins in the blood [B1]
So the water potential of the blood is higher (lower oncotic pressure) [B1]
Less water returns to capillaries, so tissue fluid accumulates [B1]

questions.prompt:
Leghaemoglobin in root nodules has a hyperbolic oxygen dissociation curve similar to myoglobin, not sigmoid like haemoglobin.

Explain how this shows its structure is more like myoglobin. (3)
hints: Sigmoid curves come from cooperative binding.
questions.solution:
Haemoglobin has four subunits; binding of one O₂ changes its shape, making it easier for the next to bind (cooperative binding) — sigmoid curve [B1]
Myoglobin has a single subunit, so no cooperative binding — hyperbolic curve [B1]
So leghaemoglobin probably has one subunit / binds one O₂, like myoglobin [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why myoglobin's high affinity for oxygen is useful in muscle. (3)
hints: Releases only at very low pO₂.
questions.solution:
Myoglobin has a higher affinity for O₂ than haemoglobin (curve to the left) [B1]
So it takes O₂ from haemoglobin and stores it in muscle [B1]
Releases O₂ only when pO₂ is very low, e.g. during intense exercise [B1]

questions.prompt: Llamas live at high altitude. Explain why their haemoglobin has a higher affinity for oxygen than human haemoglobin. (3)
questions.solution:
Partial pressure of oxygen is low at high altitude [B1]
Higher affinity means haemoglobin can still become saturated in the lungs [B1]
Curve shifted to the left [B1]

questions.prompt:
The rate of photosynthesis of leaves was given in µmol m⁻² s⁻¹.

Describe what could have been measured to determine this rate. (3)
hints: Which gas is taken up or given out?
Per unit area per unit time.
questions.solution:
Uptake of CO₂ (or release of O₂) [B1]
Measured in micromoles (amount of gas) [B1]
Per square metre of leaf area per second [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why the rate of oxygen production by a plant is lower than its true rate of photosynthesis. (3)
questions.solution:
Plants also respire, using some of the oxygen produced [B1]
Measured oxygen production = photosynthesis minus respiration (net) [B1]
Some oxygen may dissolve / stay in air spaces [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how leaf discs can be used to measure the rate of photosynthesis. (3)
questions.solution:
Air is removed from leaf discs (vacuum / syringe) in sodium hydrogencarbonate solution so they sink [B1]
In light, discs produce oxygen, which fills air spaces so they float [B1]
Time taken for discs to float measures rate (faster = higher rate) [B1]

questions.prompt:
At low light intensities, GM plants with wider stomata photosynthesised at the same rate as normal plants. At high light intensities, GM plants had a higher rate.

Explain these results. (3)
hints: What is limiting at low light?
At high light, what becomes limiting?
questions.solution:
At low light intensity, light is the limiting factor, so wider stomata have no effect [B1]
At high light, CO₂ becomes limiting [B1]
Wider stomata let more CO₂ diffuse in, so GM plants photosynthesise faster [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why increasing temperature has little effect on the rate of photosynthesis at low light intensity. (3)
questions.solution:
Light is the limiting factor [B1]
Light-dependent reactions produce too little ATP and reduced NADP [B1]
So faster Calvin cycle enzymes (from higher temperature) can't increase the rate [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why the rate of photosynthesis levels off at high light intensities. (3)
questions.solution:
Another factor becomes limiting, e.g. CO₂ concentration or temperature [B1]
Enzymes of the Calvin cycle (RuBisCO) working at maximum rate [B1]
All chlorophyll / photosystems saturated with light [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why wider stomata in GM crops could increase yield. (3)
questions.solution:
More CO₂ diffuses into the leaf [B1]
More CO₂ fixed in the Calvin cycle / more GALP and glucose made [B1]
More carbohydrate for growth / biomass, so higher yield [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest why GM crops with wider stomata might have lower yields in dry conditions. (3)
questions.solution:
More water lost by transpiration through wider stomata [B1]
Plant may wilt / close stomata, reducing CO₂ uptake [B1]
Less photosynthesis, so lower yield [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe three adaptations of xerophytes that reduce water loss. (3)
questions.solution:
Sunken stomata / hairs trap humid air, reducing the water potential gradient [B1]
Rolled leaves enclose stomata [B1]
Thick waxy cuticle [B1]
Reduced leaf surface area (spines / needles) [B1]
Any 3 — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt: State what is meant by an ecosystem. (1)
questions.solution: All the organisms (community) in an area and the non-living (abiotic) components, interacting [B1]

questions.prompt: State what is meant by a community. (1)
questions.solution: All the populations of different species living in the same area at the same time [B1]

questions.prompt: State what is meant by a population. (1)
questions.solution: All the organisms of one species living in an area at the same time [B1]

questions.prompt:
A volcanic island formed in the sea in 1965. By 2000, many plant species had colonised it.

Explain how ecosystems have developed on the island since it formed. (5)
questions.solution:
Primary succession on bare rock with no soil [B1]
Pioneer species (lichens, mosses) colonise, arriving as spores / seeds by wind, sea or birds [B1]
They weather rock and add organic matter when they die, forming soil [B1]
Conditions change, so new species (grasses, then shrubs) can colonise and outcompete pioneers [B1]
Biodiversity and biomass increase over time [B1]
Towards a climax community [B1]
Any 5 — max 5 marks.

questions.prompt: Describe secondary succession after a forest fire, and explain why it is faster than primary succession. (5)
questions.solution:
Soil remains after the fire, so pioneer stage is skipped [B1]
Seeds and roots survive in the soil [B1]
Fast-growing plants (grasses, herbs) colonise first [B1]
Followed by shrubs, then trees as conditions change [B1]
Faster because soil, nutrients and seed bank are already present [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why conservation of heathland or grassland often involves managing succession. (5)
hints: Left alone, what would it become?
questions.solution:
Without management, succession would continue to woodland (climax) [B1]
Heathland / grassland species would be outcompeted and lost [B1]
Deflected succession maintains a plagioclimax [B1]
Methods: grazing, mowing, controlled burning, removing scrub [B1]
Maintains habitats and biodiversity of species adapted to these conditions [B1]

questions.prompt:
After large numbers of seagulls began nesting on part of the island, the number of plant species there rose much faster than elsewhere.

Comment on the effect of the gulls. (4)
hints: What do gulls add to soil?
questions.solution:
Gull droppings add nitrogen and phosphate to the soil [B1]
Gulls bring seeds from elsewhere [B1]
More nutrients allow more species to grow / faster soil formation [B1]
Correlation only; other factors could contribute [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the role of bacteria in the nitrogen cycle. (4)
questions.solution:
Nitrogen-fixing bacteria convert N₂ into ammonium / ammonia [B1]
Saprobionts decompose organic matter, releasing ammonium (ammonification) [B1]
Nitrifying bacteria convert ammonium to nitrites then nitrates [B1]
Denitrifying bacteria convert nitrates to N₂ in anaerobic soil [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why ploughing and draining fields increases the nitrate content of the soil. (4)
questions.solution:
Ploughing / draining aerates the soil [B1]
Nitrifying bacteria are aerobic, so more ammonium converted to nitrate [B1]
Denitrifying bacteria are anaerobic, so less nitrate lost [B1]
More nitrate available for plants [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the part of a chloroplast where the light-dependent stage occurs. (1)
questions.solution: Thylakoid membranes (grana) [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the space inside a chloroplast where hydrogen ions accumulate during the light-dependent stage. (1)
questions.solution: Thylakoid space (lumen) [B1]

questions.prompt: Where in a chloroplast are proteins translated? (1)
questions.solution: On 70S ribosomes in the stroma [B1]

questions.prompt: Give suitable units for the rate of photosynthesis measured as carbon dioxide uptake by leaves. (1)
questions.solution: µmol CO₂ m⁻² s⁻¹ (or mg CO₂ dm⁻² h⁻¹) [B1]

questions.prompt: Give suitable units for the rate of oxygen production by pondweed measured in a photosynthometer. (1)
questions.solution: mm³ min⁻¹ (or cm³ h⁻¹ g⁻¹) [B1]

questions.prompt: Give suitable units for net primary productivity. (1)
questions.solution: kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹ [B1]

questions.prompt:
The rate of photosynthesis was measured at leaf temperatures from 10 °C to 40 °C at high and low CO₂. At high CO₂, rate rose to a peak of 30 units at 30 °C, then fell. At low CO₂, rate rose to only 12 units at 25 °C, then fell slightly.

Give three conclusions. (3)
questions.solution:
Rate is higher at high CO₂ at all temperatures above 10 °C [B1]
Rate increases with temperature up to an optimum, then decreases [B1]
Optimum temperature is higher at high CO₂ (30 °C vs 25 °C) [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why the rate of photosynthesis falls at high temperatures even when CO₂ and light are not limiting. (3)
questions.solution:
Enzymes such as RuBisCO begin to denature [B1]
RuBisCO binds O₂ more readily at high temperatures (photorespiration), so less CO₂ is fixed [B1]
Stomata may close to reduce water loss, so less CO₂ enters [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why commercial growers increase both CO₂ and temperature in glasshouses, rather than only one. (3)
questions.solution:
Raising one factor only increases the rate until another becomes limiting [B1]
Raising both increases the maximum rate / optimum temperature is higher at high CO₂ [B1]
Growers balance the cost of heating / CO₂ against the extra yield [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain the effects of CO₂ concentration and temperature on the rate of formation of GALP. (4)
hints: CO₂ is a substrate for RuBisCO.
questions.solution:
More CO₂ means more CO₂ combines with RuBP, forming more GP [B1]
More GP is reduced to GALP using ATP and reduced NADP [B1]
Higher temperature (up to the optimum) increases kinetic energy and enzyme–substrate complexes [B1]
Above the optimum, enzymes denature, so less GALP is made [B1]

questions.prompt: Predict and explain the changes in concentrations of GP and RuBP when a plant is moved from light into darkness. (4)
questions.solution:
In the dark, no ATP or reduced NADP is made [B1]
GP cannot be reduced to GALP, so GP accumulates [B1]
RuBP is not regenerated (needs ATP) [B1]
But RuBP is still used up combining with CO₂, so RuBP concentration falls [B1]

questions.prompt: Predict and explain the changes in GP and RuBP concentrations when CO₂ concentration falls. (4)
hints: RuBP has less CO₂ to combine with.
questions.solution:
Less CO₂ combines with RuBP, so less GP is formed [B1]
GP is still reduced to GALP, so GP concentration falls [B1]
RuBP is still regenerated from GALP [B1]
But less is used, so RuBP accumulates [B1]

questions.prompt:
Hypoxia-inducible factors (HIFs) are transcription factors made when cells are short of oxygen.

Explain how HIFs could increase the rate of glycolysis. (2)
questions.solution:
HIF binds to promoters of genes for glycolytic enzymes / glucose transporters [B1]
Increasing transcription, so more enzymes are made and glycolysis is faster [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how a transcription factor can switch a gene on. (2)
questions.solution:
Transcription factor binds to the promoter / a specific DNA sequence [B1]
Helps RNA polymerase bind, so the gene is transcribed [B1]

questions.prompt: In hypoxia, HIFs increase transcription of the gene for erythropoietin (EPO). Explain how this helps the body cope with low oxygen. (2)
questions.solution:
EPO stimulates bone marrow to produce more red blood cells [B1]
More haemoglobin to carry oxygen to tissues [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why cells respond to low oxygen by increasing the rate of glycolysis. (4)
questions.solution:
Without oxygen, the electron transport chain stops (no final acceptor) [B1]
So the Krebs cycle and link reaction stop as NAD is not regenerated [B1]
Glycolysis is the only source of ATP, producing only 2 ATP per glucose [B1]
Faster glycolysis gives enough ATP; pyruvate converted to lactate to regenerate NAD [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe what happens in the Krebs cycle. (4)
questions.solution:
Acetyl CoA combines with oxaloacetate (4C) to form citrate (6C) [B1]
Citrate is decarboxylated and dehydrogenated, releasing CO₂ [B1]
Reduced NAD and reduced FAD are produced [B1]
One ATP made by substrate-level phosphorylation; oxaloacetate regenerated [B1]

questions.prompt: Compare anaerobic respiration in mammals and in yeast. (4)
questions.solution:
Both involve glycolysis followed by regeneration of NAD [B1]
Mammals reduce pyruvate to lactate [B1]
Yeast converts pyruvate to ethanal (releasing CO₂), then to ethanol [B1]
Lactate can be converted back to pyruvate; ethanol production is irreversible [B1]

questions.prompt:
As a glacier melts, it leaves bare rock. Areas uncovered for longer have deeper soil, more nitrate and more leaf litter.

Explain how succession brings about these changes in the soil. (5)
questions.solution:
Pioneer species (lichens, mosses) colonise bare rock [B1]
Weathering of rock and death / decomposition of pioneers forms thin soil [B1]
Larger plants colonise; more biomass means more leaf litter and organic matter [B1]
Nitrogen-fixing plants / bacteria and decomposers increase nitrate in the soil [B1]
Deeper roots break up rock and soil depth increases over time [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how leaf litter is decomposed and how this increases soil fertility. (5)
questions.solution:
Detritivores (e.g. earthworms) break leaves into smaller pieces, increasing surface area [B1]
Saprobionts (bacteria, fungi) secrete enzymes and digest organic matter extracellularly [B1]
Absorb products and respire, releasing CO₂ [B1]
Ammonification releases ammonium; nitrifying bacteria convert it to nitrate [B1]
Minerals (nitrate, phosphate) are available for plant uptake [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why biodiversity usually increases during succession, but may fall slightly at the climax stage. (5)
questions.solution:
Each stage changes conditions (soil, shelter, nutrients) [B1]
More habitats and niches become available [B1]
More food sources for animals [B1]
At the climax, a few dominant species (e.g. trees) may outcompete others [B1]
e.g. shading reduces ground plants, so diversity may fall slightly [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how leghaemoglobin enables legumes to grow in waterlogged and compacted soils. (3)
hints: Bacteria still need oxygen to respire.
questions.solution:
Leghaemoglobin binds oxygen, keeping free oxygen low in the nodule, so nitrogenase is not inhibited [B1]
But supplies enough oxygen to the bacteria for aerobic respiration to make ATP for nitrogen fixation [B1]
So nitrogen is fixed into ammonium even where soil nitrate is low (waterlogged soils have denitrification) [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why the relationship between Rhizobium bacteria and legume plants is mutualistic. (3)
questions.solution:
Bacteria fix nitrogen, providing the plant with ammonium for amino acids [B1]
Plant provides bacteria with carbohydrates (sugars) and a protected environment [B1]
Both organisms benefit [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why farmers grow legumes such as clover in rotation with cereal crops. (3)
questions.solution:
Legumes have nitrogen-fixing bacteria in root nodules [B1]
When ploughed in, they decompose and increase soil nitrate [B1]
Reduces the need for artificial fertiliser for the next crop [B1]

questions.prompt:
During the log phase, the number of bacteria in sucrose rose from log₁₀ 4 to log₁₀ 7 cells cm⁻³, and in glucose from log₁₀ 4 to log₁₀ 6, over the same time.

Calculate how many times faster the bacteria increased in sucrose. (2)
questions.solution:
Sucrose: 10⁷ ÷ 10⁴ = 1000-fold; glucose: 10⁶ ÷ 10⁴ = 100-fold [M1]
10 times faster in sucrose [A1]

questions.prompt: A bacterium divides every 20 minutes. Starting with 50 cells, calculate the number after 3 hours. (2)
questions.solution:
180 ÷ 20 = 9 generations [M1]
50 × 2⁹ = 25 600 cells [A1]

questions.prompt:
A culture grew from 2.0 × 10³ to 6.4 × 10⁴ cells cm⁻³ in 100 minutes.

Calculate the number of generations and the mean generation time. (2)
questions.solution:
32 = 2⁵, so 5 generations [M1]
100 ÷ 5 = 20 minutes [A1]

questions.prompt: Bacteria grown with sucrose had a longer lag phase than those grown with glucose. Suggest why. (2)
hints: Sucrose must be broken down first.
questions.solution:
Sucrose must be hydrolysed to glucose and fructose before it can be used [B1]
Bacteria must first synthesise the enzyme (sucrase / invertase) — genes switched on [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe and explain the stationary phase of a bacterial growth curve. (2)
questions.solution:
Rate of cell division equals rate of cell death [B1]
Because nutrients run low / toxic waste builds up / space limited [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why the death phase occurs in a closed culture of bacteria. (2)
questions.solution:
Nutrients are used up [B1]
Toxic waste products accumulate, so death rate exceeds division rate [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why measuring turbidity (cloudiness) with a colorimeter gives different results from dilution plating. (1)
questions.solution: Turbidity measures total cells (living and dead), while dilution plating counts only viable (living) cells [B1]

questions.prompt:
A sample was diluted 10⁶ times and 0.1 cm³ was spread on a plate. 42 colonies grew.

Calculate the number of viable bacteria per cm³ in the original sample. (1)
Why is a plate with between 30 and 300 colonies preferred for counting? (1)
questions.solution: Fewer than 30 is unreliable / not representative; more than 300 colonies overlap and can't be counted accurately [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the genus of fungus that causes stem rust of wheat. (1)
questions.solution: Puccinia [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the type of pathogen that causes tobacco mosaic disease. (1)
hints: It has RNA and a protein coat.
questions.solution: Virus (tobacco mosaic virus) [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the genus of protoctist that causes malaria. (1)
questions.solution: Plasmodium [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how infection of wheat by stem rust fungus reduces grain yield. (3)
hints: The fungus feeds on the plant.
What happens to photosynthesis and transport?
questions.solution:
Fungus uses / absorbs the plant's sugars and nutrients [B1]
Damages leaves and stems, reducing area for photosynthesis [B1]
Disrupts xylem / phloem, so less water and sugar transported [B1]
Less glucose for grain formation / stems break [B1]
Any 3 — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt: Explain how tobacco mosaic virus reduces the growth of tobacco plants. (3)
questions.solution:
Virus infects leaf cells and damages chloroplasts [B1]
Leaves become mottled / discoloured, so less chlorophyll [B1]
Less photosynthesis, so less sugar for growth / stunted growth [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe three ways in which plants physically or chemically defend themselves against pathogens. (3)
questions.solution:
Waxy cuticle / cellulose cell wall acts as a barrier [B1]
Callose deposited to block plasmodesmata / sieve plates [B1]
Production of antimicrobial chemicals, e.g. tannins, phenols, saponins [B1]
Lignin thickening of cell walls [B1]
Any 3 — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt: Explain why scientists looked for MHC molecules on cells they thought could present antigens to T cells. (2)
hints: T cells only recognise antigens in a certain form.
questions.solution:
Antigens are presented on the cell surface bound to MHC proteins [B1]
T cells only recognise antigens combined with MHC, so cells without MHC can't activate them [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how a macrophage acts as an antigen-presenting cell. (2)
questions.solution:
Macrophage engulfs and digests the pathogen [B1]
Displays antigens on its surface combined with MHC proteins, for T helper cells to bind [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how the immune system distinguishes body cells from foreign cells. (2)
questions.solution:
Body cells have self antigens / MHC proteins that the immune system recognises [B1]
Foreign cells have different (non-self) antigens that lymphocytes with complementary receptors bind to [B1]

questions.prompt:
Radioactivity in T lymphocytes (arbitrary units):
Antigen X: with antigen 80, without 10
Antigen Y: with antigen 75, without 12
Antigen Z: with antigen 14, without 11

State the conclusions that can be drawn. (3)
questions.solution:
X and Y caused much more T cell division than controls [B1]
So endothelial cells can present antigens X and Y to T cells [B1]
Z had little effect — not presented / no T cells specific to Z [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the roles of T helper cells and T killer cells in the immune response. (3)
questions.solution:
T helper cells bind to presented antigens and release cytokines [B1]
Cytokines activate B cells (to clone and make plasma cells) and T killer cells [B1]
T killer cells bind to infected body cells and release perforin, destroying them [B1]

questions.prompt: In multiple sclerosis, T cells attack myelin. Explain why this slows nerve impulses. (3)
questions.solution:
Myelin sheath insulates the axon [B1]
Loss of myelin means depolarisation happens along the whole axon, not just at nodes [B1]
No saltatory conduction, so impulses slower or blocked [B1]

questions.prompt:
(i) Name one Gram-negative bacterium. (1)
(ii) Give one structural difference between Gram-negative and Gram-positive bacteria. (1)
hints: E. coli is a common example.
Think about the peptidoglycan layer and outer membrane.
questions.solution:
(i) Escherichia coli / Salmonella / Neisseria [B1]
(ii) Gram-negative have a thin peptidoglycan wall plus an outer membrane (lipopolysaccharide); Gram-positive have a thick peptidoglycan wall and no outer membrane [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the colours seen after Gram staining and explain why the two types of bacteria stain differently. (2)
questions.solution:
Gram-positive stain purple / violet; Gram-negative stain red / pink [B1]
Thick peptidoglycan in Gram-positive retains crystal violet; thin wall / outer membrane in Gram-negative lets it wash out so they take up the red counterstain [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why Gram-negative bacteria are often less affected by penicillin than Gram-positive bacteria. (2)
hints: What stops it reaching the wall?
questions.solution:
Penicillin prevents formation of cross-links in peptidoglycan [B1]
The outer membrane of Gram-negative bacteria stops penicillin reaching the cell wall [B1]

questions.prompt:
The LD50 of a toxin is 11 ng per kg of body mass. A rat has a mass of 280 g.

Calculate the mass of toxin that would kill half of a group of such rats. (1)
State what is meant by the LD50 of a toxin. (1)
questions.solution: The dose that kills 50 % of a test population [B1]

questions.prompt: A toxin has an LD50 of 2.5 µg kg⁻¹. Calculate the dose for a 70 kg person, in mg. (1)
State two differences between endotoxins and exotoxins, other than toxicity. (2)
questions.solution:
Endotoxins are part of the outer membrane (lipopolysaccharide) of Gram-negative bacteria; exotoxins are secreted proteins [B1]
Endotoxins are released when bacteria die / lyse; exotoxins are released by living bacteria; endotoxins are heat-stable [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how cholera toxin causes diarrhoea. (2)
hints: It affects ion channels in the gut.
questions.solution:
Toxin causes chloride channels in intestinal epithelial cells to stay open, so Cl⁻ is secreted into the lumen [B1]
Water potential of the lumen falls, so water moves out of cells by osmosis — watery diarrhoea [B1]

questions.prompt: Give two ways in which bacteria cause disease. (2)
questions.solution:
Release toxins that damage host cells / disrupt their function [B1]
Invade and destroy host cells / use host nutrients [B1]

questions.prompt:
One way to control malaria uses a GM fungus that kills mosquitoes. Another uses a non-lethal fungus that stops Plasmodium developing inside mosquitoes.

Explain why the non-lethal approach is less controversial. (3)
questions.solution:
Mosquitoes are not killed, so food chains (e.g. for bats, fish) are not disrupted [B1]
Less selection pressure for mosquitoes to become resistant [B1]
Not genetically modified, so fewer concerns about spread of toxin genes / harm to other species [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe three methods used to reduce the spread of malaria. (3)
questions.solution:
Insecticide-treated bed nets [B1]
Draining standing water / spraying insecticides to kill mosquitoes and larvae [B1]
Antimalarial drugs for prevention and treatment [B1]
Vaccination (e.g. RTS,S) [B1]
Any 3 — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt: Explain why it has been difficult to develop a vaccine against malaria. (3)
hints: Plasmodium has a complex life cycle.
questions.solution:
Plasmodium has several life stages with different antigens [B1]
It spends time inside liver cells and red blood cells, hidden from antibodies [B1]
Its antigens show variation / it is a eukaryote with many genes [B1]

questions.prompt:
When bacteria were infected with phages, the number of lysed cells did not increase for about 30 minutes, then rose rapidly.

Explain the delay. (3)
hints: What must happen inside the cell first?
questions.solution:
Phages must attach and inject their DNA [B1]
Phage DNA is replicated and phage proteins are made using the bacterium's enzymes and ribosomes [B1]
New phages are assembled before the cell lyses [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why bacteriophages could be used to treat bacterial infections that are resistant to antibiotics. (3)
questions.solution:
Phages infect and lyse bacteria, including antibiotic-resistant strains [B1]
They are specific, so don't harm human cells / normal flora [B1]
They replicate at the site of infection, increasing in number while bacteria are present [B1]

questions.prompt: Compare the lytic and lysogenic cycles of a bacteriophage. (3)
hints: Is the cell destroyed straight away?
questions.solution:
Lytic: phage DNA is replicated immediately and the cell bursts [B1]
Lysogenic: phage DNA is inserted into the bacterial chromosome (prophage) and replicated with it [B1]
Lysogenic phage can later enter the lytic cycle [B1]

questions.prompt:
During phagocytosis, the breakdown of actin filaments releases soluble monomers in part of a macrophage. Water then flows into that part of the cell.

Explain why. (2)
questions.solution:
More solute particles lower the water potential in that part of the cell [B1]
Water moves in by osmosis from higher to lower water potential [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why red blood cells burst when placed in distilled water but plant cells do not. (2)
questions.solution:
Water enters both by osmosis as the water potential outside is higher [B1]
Plant cell wall resists expansion (turgor), while red blood cells have no wall so they burst [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how a macrophage engulfs and destroys a bacterium. (2)
questions.solution:
Macrophage surrounds the bacterium with pseudopodia, enclosing it in a phagosome / vacuole [B1]
Lysosomes fuse with the phagosome and release enzymes (lysozyme) that digest the bacterium [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the events after phagocytosis that lead to T helper cells being activated. (3)
questions.solution:
Bacterium digested; antigens combined with MHC proteins [B1]
Presented on the macrophage surface (antigen-presenting cell) [B1]
T helper cell with a complementary receptor binds, is activated and divides [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how antibodies make phagocytosis more effective. (3)
questions.solution:
Antibodies bind to antigens on pathogens, acting as opsonins / markers [B1]
Phagocytes have receptors for the antibody, so bind pathogens more easily [B1]
Antibodies cause agglutination, clumping pathogens together [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how the structure of an antibody is related to its function. (3)
questions.solution:
Four polypeptide chains (two heavy, two light) held by disulfide bridges [B1]
Variable regions form antigen-binding sites complementary to one antigen [B1]
Two binding sites allow agglutination; hinge region gives flexibility; constant region binds phagocytes [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why DNA fragments can be separated by gel electrophoresis. (2)
hints: Do all fragments move at the same speed?
questions.solution:
DNA is negatively charged (phosphate groups), so moves towards the positive electrode [B1]
Smaller fragments move faster / further through the gel [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the stages of the polymerase chain reaction (PCR). (2)
questions.solution:
Heat to 95 °C to separate the strands; cool to about 55 °C so primers anneal [B1]
Heat to 72 °C — Taq DNA polymerase adds complementary nucleotides; repeat cycles [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why short tandem repeats (STRs) are used in DNA profiling. (2)
hints: Different numbers of repeats give different fragment lengths.
questions.solution:
The number of repeats at each STR locus varies between individuals [B1]
So fragments of different lengths are produced, giving a pattern unique to each person (except identical twins) [B1]

questions.prompt:
Doxorubicin is a cancer drug that inserts between DNA bases, holding the two strands together. It also binds to an enzyme used for DNA repair.
