Explain how doxorubicin prevents cancer cells from dividing. (5)
hints: What must happen to DNA before division?
What happens if damage can't be repaired?
questions.solution:
The two DNA strands cannot separate [B1]
So DNA helicase can't unwind DNA / DNA polymerase can't replicate it [B1]
No DNA replication in S phase, so cell cannot enter mitosis [B1]
Transcription also prevented, so proteins needed for division are not made [B1]
DNA damage is not repaired, so checkpoints stop the cycle / apoptosis occurs [B1]
questions.subtopic: Cancer drugs and the cell cycle

questions.prompt: Describe the process of semi-conservative DNA replication. (5)
questions.solution:
DNA helicase breaks hydrogen bonds, separating the strands [B1]
Each strand acts as a template [B1]
Free DNA nucleotides pair with complementary bases [B1]
DNA polymerase joins nucleotides, forming phosphodiester bonds [B1]
Each new molecule has one original and one new strand [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how mutations in proto-oncogenes and tumour suppressor genes can lead to cancer. (5)
questions.solution:
Proto-oncogenes stimulate cell division [B1]
A mutation can turn them into oncogenes, permanently switched on [B1]
Tumour suppressor genes slow division / trigger apoptosis [B1]
Mutation inactivates them, so division isn't stopped [B1]
Uncontrolled mitosis forms a tumour [B1]

questions.prompt:
Write the mRNA sequence transcribed from this DNA template strand:

TACGGATCA (1)
hints: A pairs with U in RNA.
questions.solution: AUGCCUAGU [B1]

questions.prompt: An mRNA codon is GCA. Give the anticodon on the tRNA that pairs with it. (1)
questions.solution: CGU [B1]

questions.prompt: A DNA template strand reads CCTAAG. Give the sequence of the coding (non-template) strand of DNA. (1)
hints: Coding strand is complementary to the template.
questions.solution: GGATTC [B1]

questions.prompt: Some amino acids are coded for by more than one codon. Name this property of the genetic code. (1)
questions.solution: Degenerate [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain what is meant by the genetic code being non-overlapping. (1)
questions.solution: Each base is part of only one triplet / codon; codons are read one after another [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why the genetic code being universal allows human genes to be expressed in bacteria. (1)
questions.solution: The same codons code for the same amino acids in all organisms, so bacteria make the same protein [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how a fungus could be genetically modified to produce a spider toxin that kills mosquitoes. (3)
questions.solution:
Cut the toxin gene from spider DNA using restriction enzymes (or make it from mRNA with reverse transcriptase) [B1]
Insert it into a vector (e.g. plasmid / Agrobacterium) with sticky ends and DNA ligase, with a promoter [B1]
Transfer the vector into fungal cells and select modified cells using a marker gene [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how restriction enzymes and DNA ligase are used to produce recombinant DNA. (3)
questions.solution:
The same restriction enzyme cuts the gene and the plasmid at specific recognition sequences [B1]
Producing complementary sticky ends [B1]
Sticky ends pair by base pairing; DNA ligase joins the sugar–phosphate backbones [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why marker genes are used when genetically modifying cells. (3)
hints: Not all cells take up the plasmid.
questions.solution:
Only a small proportion of cells take up the recombinant DNA [B1]
Marker gene (e.g. antibiotic resistance / GFP) is inserted alongside the desired gene [B1]
Cells are grown on antibiotic / viewed under UV, so only transformed cells survive / glow [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the bond that holds complementary bases together in DNA. (1)
questions.solution: Hydrogen bonds [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the bond that joins the sugar of one nucleotide to the phosphate of the next. (1)
questions.solution: Phosphodiester bond [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain what is meant by DNA strands being antiparallel. (1)
questions.solution: The two strands run in opposite directions — one 5′ to 3′, the other 3′ to 5′ [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the roles of three named enzymes involved in DNA replication. (3)
questions.solution:
DNA helicase — unwinds the double helix and breaks hydrogen bonds between bases [B1]
DNA polymerase — joins nucleotides to the new strand, forming phosphodiester bonds [B1]
DNA ligase — joins Okazaki fragments on the lagging strand [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how the Meselson–Stahl experiment showed that DNA replication is semi-conservative. (3)
hints: Bands after one and two generations.
questions.solution:
Bacteria grown in ¹⁵N (heavy) medium, then transferred to ¹⁴N (light) [B1]
After one generation, DNA formed a single intermediate band — each molecule had one heavy and one light strand [B1]
After two generations, half intermediate, half light — consistent only with semi-conservative replication [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why DNA replication must be accurate, and how errors can arise. (3)
questions.solution:
Daughter cells need identical genetic information to make the correct proteins [B1]
Errors (e.g. wrong base inserted) cause mutations [B1]
Mutation rate increased by mutagens such as UV or chemicals; proofreading by DNA polymerase reduces errors [B1]

questions.prompt:
A section of double-stranded DNA contains 10 000 nucleotides. 35 % of them contain adenine.

Calculate the number of cytosine nucleotides. (2)

A DNA molecule has 4000 base pairs. 1200 of the bases are guanine.

Calculate the number of adenine bases. (2)
In one strand of DNA, 20 % of bases are A and 30 % are T. What percentage of bases in the complementary strand are A? (2)
hints: A in one strand pairs with T in the other.
Single strands don't follow A = T.
questions.solution:
T in the first strand pairs with A in the complementary strand [M1]
So 30 % [A1]

questions.prompt:
Wheat was genetically modified to be resistant to stem rust, but after some years the GM wheat became infected. Spores of the fungus are produced in huge numbers and the fungus reproduces sexually on another host plant.

Deduce why the resistance was lost. (3)
hints: The fungus has lots of genetic variation.
Natural selection acts on the fungus.
questions.solution:
Mutation / sexual reproduction on the second host produces genetic variation in the fungus [B1]
A fungus with an allele that overcomes the resistance survives on GM wheat [B1]
It reproduces, producing many spores, so the new strain spreads [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how a population of insects becomes resistant to an insecticide. (3)
questions.solution:
Random mutation gives some insects an allele for resistance [B1]
Insecticide kills non-resistant insects; resistant ones survive and reproduce [B1]
Resistant allele passed on, so its frequency increases over generations [B1]

questions.prompt: Suggest three ways farmers could slow the evolution of resistance to a pesticide. (3)
questions.solution:
Use pesticides only when needed / lower amounts [B1]
Rotate between different pesticides with different modes of action [B1]
Leave refuges of untreated crops so susceptible pests survive and breed [B1]
Use biological control / integrated pest management [B1]
Any 3 — max 3 marks.

questions.prompt:
Siamese cats have a mutation in the gene for the enzyme tyrosinase, which makes dark fur pigment. The mutant enzyme is denatured at normal body temperature.

Explain why the cooler parts of the body (ears, paws, tail) have dark fur. (3)
hints: The enzyme only works when cool.
questions.solution:
The mutant enzyme has a different tertiary structure that is unstable at higher temperatures [B1]
At warmer body regions, it denatures, so no pigment is made — light fur [B1]
At cooler extremities, enzyme keeps its shape and makes pigment — dark fur [B1]

questions.prompt: Hydrangea plants have blue flowers in acidic soil and pink flowers in alkaline soil. Explain how this shows that phenotype is affected by both genotype and environment. (3)
questions.solution:
Plants with the same genotype produce different flower colours [B1]
Soil pH (environment) affects the pigment / aluminium uptake [B1]
So phenotype results from the interaction of genotype and environment [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why human height shows continuous variation. (3)
questions.solution:
Height is controlled by many genes (polygenic) [B1]
Each gene has a small additive effect [B1]
Environment (e.g. diet) also affects height, giving a range of values [B1]

questions.prompt:
In maize, smooth (A) is dominant to wrinkled (a) and purple (B) is dominant to yellow (b).

Give all possible genotypes of a smooth, purple grain. (1)
hints: At least one A and one B.
questions.solution: AABB, AABb, AaBB, AaBb [B1]

questions.prompt: Give all possible gametes produced by a plant with genotype AaBb (genes on different chromosomes). (1)
questions.solution: AB, Ab, aB, ab [B1]

questions.prompt: Give the genotype of a wrinkled, yellow maize grain. (1)
questions.solution: aabb [B1]

questions.prompt:
Two wrinkled, purple maize plants were crossed. The offspring were wrinkled purple and wrinkled yellow.

Give the genotypes of the parents. (1)
questions.solution: aaBb × aaBb [B1]

questions.prompt: A smooth, purple plant crossed with a wrinkled, yellow plant produced only smooth, purple offspring. Give the genotype of the smooth, purple parent. (1)
questions.solution: AABB [B1]

questions.prompt: Give the expected phenotype ratio from a cross between two AaBb plants. (1)
questions.solution: 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 (smooth purple : smooth yellow : wrinkled purple : wrinkled yellow) [B1]

questions.prompt:
A smooth, purple plant (AaBb) is crossed with a wrinkled, yellow plant (aabb).

Use a genetic diagram to find the probability of producing wrinkled, purple grains. (4)
hints: AaBb makes four gametes; aabb makes one.
questions.solution:
Gametes AB, Ab, aB, ab and ab [M1]
Offspring: AaBb, Aabb, aaBb, aabb [M1]
Phenotypes 1 smooth purple : 1 smooth yellow : 1 wrinkled purple : 1 wrinkled yellow [A1]
Probability of wrinkled purple = 0.25 [A1]

questions.prompt:
In guinea pigs, black (B) is dominant to white (b) and rough coat (R) is dominant to smooth (r). Two BbRr guinea pigs are crossed.

Calculate the probability of offspring being white and rough. (4)
hints: Use a 4 × 4 Punnett square, or multiply probabilities.
questions.solution:
Each parent produces BR, Br, bR, br gametes [M1]
P(bb) = 1/4 [M1]
P(R_) = 3/4 [M1]
P(white, rough) = 3/16 [A1]

questions.prompt:
A test cross of AaBb × aabb produced 180 AaBb, 20 Aabb, 22 aaBb and 178 aabb.

Explain why these results differ from the expected ratio. (4)
questions.solution:
Expected ratio 1 : 1 : 1 : 1 (100 each) [B1]
Parental combinations (AB and ab) are most common [B1]
So the genes are linked — on the same chromosome [B1]
Recombinants (Ab and aB) only arise by crossing over, which is rare between close loci [B1]

questions.prompt:
In an isolated population of 1400 people, 14 have a recessive genetic disorder.

Use the Hardy-Weinberg equation to calculate the number of heterozygous carriers. (4)

In a population of 2000 moths, 1280 are dark (dominant) and 720 are pale (recessive).

Calculate the number of homozygous dark moths. (4)
The frequency of a recessive allele is 0.3. Calculate the percentages of the population that are homozygous dominant, heterozygous and homozygous recessive. (4)
A genetic disorder affects 1 in 100 people in an isolated population, but only 1 in 40 000 people in general. Explain why. (2)
questions.solution:
Founder effect — a few founders happened to carry the allele, giving a high frequency [B1]
Isolation / inbreeding / genetic drift kept the frequency high, with no gene flow from other populations [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why inbreeding increases the frequency of genetic disorders caused by recessive alleles. (2)
questions.solution:
Related parents are more likely to carry the same recessive allele [B1]
So offspring more likely to be homozygous recessive and show the disorder [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how gene flow between populations affects allele frequencies. (2)
questions.solution:
Migration brings in / removes alleles [B1]
Makes allele frequencies more similar between populations / increases genetic diversity [B1]

questions.prompt: State what is meant by a dominant allele. (1)
questions.solution: An allele that is expressed in the phenotype when only one copy is present (heterozygous) [B1]

questions.prompt: State what is meant by the term locus. (1)
questions.solution: The position of a gene on a chromosome [B1]

questions.prompt: State what is meant by multiple alleles. (1)
questions.solution: A gene with more than two alleles in the population (e.g. ABO blood groups) [B1]

questions.prompt:
Tawny owls show a range of feather colours from pale grey to dark brown, scored 1 to 11.

Explain this range of colours. (2)
questions.solution:
Colour is controlled by several genes (polygenic) / codominance [B1]
Environment may also affect pigment, giving continuous variation [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why blood group shows discontinuous variation. (2)
questions.solution:
Controlled by a single gene with a few alleles [B1]
Not affected by the environment, so distinct categories (A, B, AB, O) [B1]

questions.prompt: Give two sources of genetic variation in a population. (2)
questions.solution:
Mutation creates new alleles [B1]
Meiosis (crossing over / independent assortment) and random fertilisation create new combinations [B1]

questions.prompt:
In a population of 120 owls, grey colour is caused by a recessive allele. 84 owls are grey.

Use the Hardy-Weinberg equation to calculate the number of heterozygous owls. (3)
4 % of a population of 500 snails show a recessive phenotype. Calculate the number of heterozygous snails. (3)
The frequency of a dominant allele is 0.6. In a population of 800, how many individuals show the dominant phenotype? (3)

In Finland, grey tawny owls survive better than brown owls in years with deep snow, but in years with little snow survival is similar. Mean snow depth fell between 1980 and 2007, and the percentage of brown owls rose from about 12 % in 1960 to over 40 % in 2007.

Evaluate the conclusion that increased greenhouse gases from human activity are increasing the frequency of the brown allele. (6)
hints: Build the chain, then critique it.
questions.solution:
Greenhouse gases cause global warming, so less snow [B1]
In deep snow, grey owls are better camouflaged / survive better (selection against brown) [B1]
With less snow, brown owls survive as well, so the selection pressure against them is reduced [B1]
Brown allele frequency increases as more brown owls survive and reproduce [B1]
But data show correlation only; no evidence given that the snow change is due to human greenhouse gases [B1]
Other factors (e.g. migration, prey changes) could be involved; one population studied [B1]
Level-marked (5–6 marks).

questions.prompt: Explain how the frequency of dark-winged peppered moths increased in industrial areas in the 1800s. (6)
questions.solution:
Mutation produced a dark (melanic) allele [B1]
Pollution blackened tree bark with soot [B1]
Dark moths were better camouflaged, so less likely to be eaten by birds [B1]
Dark moths survived and reproduced more [B1]
Passing on the dark allele [B1]
Allele frequency increased over generations (directional selection) [B1]
Level-marked (5–6 marks).

questions.prompt: Describe and explain stabilising, directional and disruptive selection, with an example of each. (6)
hints: Effect on the mean and range.
questions.solution:
Stabilising selection favours the average phenotype; reduces range, e.g. human birth mass [B1]
Occurs when the environment is stable [B1]
Directional selection favours one extreme, shifting the mean, e.g. antibiotic resistance [B1]
Occurs when the environment changes [B1]
Disruptive selection favours both extremes, e.g. beak sizes when two food sizes are available [B1]
Can lead to speciation [B1]
Level-marked (5–6 marks).

questions.prompt: Name the root of a spinal nerve that contains the cell bodies of sensory neurones. (1)
questions.solution: Dorsal root (dorsal root ganglion) [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the root through which motor neurones leave the spinal cord. (1)
questions.solution: Ventral root [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the type of neurone that connects sensory and motor neurones in the spinal cord. (1)
questions.solution: Relay neurone (interneurone) [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the region of the brain that controls breathing and heart rate. (1)
questions.solution: Medulla oblongata [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the region of the brain that controls body temperature and water balance. (1)
questions.solution: Hypothalamus [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the region of the brain responsible for conscious thought and voluntary movement. (1)
questions.solution: Cerebrum (cerebral cortex) [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how the resting potential is maintained in a neurone. (4)
questions.solution:
Na⁺/K⁺ pump actively transports 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in, using ATP [B1]
Membrane is more permeable to K⁺ (K⁺ channels open) [B1]
K⁺ diffuses out down its concentration gradient [B1]
Inside negative relative to outside — about −70 mV [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the sequence of events that produces an action potential. (4)
questions.solution:
Stimulus opens some Na⁺ channels; if threshold (about −55 mV) is reached, voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open [B1]
Na⁺ floods in, depolarising the membrane to about +40 mV [B1]
Na⁺ channels close; voltage-gated K⁺ channels open, K⁺ diffuses out (repolarisation) [B1]
Hyperpolarisation, then Na⁺/K⁺ pump restores the resting potential [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why a nerve impulse travels faster in a neurone with a larger diameter, and at higher temperatures (up to a point). (4)
questions.solution:
Larger diameter means less resistance to the flow of ions in the cytoplasm [B1]
So local currents spread further / depolarise the next region faster [B1]
Higher temperature increases the rate of diffusion of ions [B1]
But very high temperatures denature membrane proteins (channels and pumps) [B1]

questions.prompt:
Tetrodotoxin blocks voltage-gated sodium channels. When a neurone treated with tetrodotoxin was stimulated, the potential difference stayed at −70 mV.

Explain this result and why animals injected with tetrodotoxin by predators become paralysed. (4)
questions.solution:
Na⁺ channels can't open, so Na⁺ can't diffuse in [B1]
No depolarisation / threshold not reached, so no action potential (stays at resting potential) [B1]
No impulses reach the neuromuscular junction / no acetylcholine released [B1]
Muscles don't contract, so prey is paralysed (including breathing muscles) [B1]

questions.prompt: Organophosphate insecticides inhibit acetylcholinesterase. Explain their effect on synaptic transmission and muscles. (4)
questions.solution:
Acetylcholinesterase can't break down acetylcholine [B1]
ACh stays bound to receptors on the postsynaptic membrane [B1]
Na⁺ channels stay open, continuous depolarisation / action potentials [B1]
Muscles stay contracted (spasm / paralysis) [B1]

questions.prompt: Lidocaine is a local anaesthetic that blocks sodium channels in sensory neurones. Explain how it prevents pain. (4)
questions.solution:
Na⁺ cannot enter sensory neurones [B1]
No depolarisation / no action potential [B1]
No impulses sent to the brain / CNS [B1]
So pain is not perceived in that area [B1]

questions.prompt: Give two effects of auxin on plant growth. (1)
questions.solution: Stimulates cell elongation in shoots and inhibits growth of side (lateral) buds (apical dominance) [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the plant growth substance that stimulates stem elongation and seed germination. (1)
questions.solution: Gibberellin [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why a shoot bends towards light. (1)
questions.solution: Auxin moves to the shaded side, causing more cell elongation there, so the shoot bends towards the light [B1]

questions.prompt:
Kalanchoe is a short-day plant; Sedum is a long-day plant. When a Sedum shoot was grafted onto a Kalanchoe plant kept in short days (10 h light, 14 h dark), both plants flowered. A flash of far-red light in the middle of the dark period had different effects on each species.

Explain these effects. (6)
hints: A chemical signal passes through the graft.
questions.solution:
Phytochrome exists as Pr and Pfr; red light converts Pr to Pfr, far-red / darkness converts Pfr to Pr [B1]
Long nights → low Pfr at dawn, which allows short-day plants to flower [B1]
Long-day plants need high Pfr (short nights) to flower [B1]
Kalanchoe flowered in short days and produced a flowering signal (florigen / FT protein) [B1]
The signal moved through the graft (in phloem) and caused Sedum to flower too [B1]
Far-red flash converts Pfr to Pr, lowering Pfr, so promoting flowering in short-day plants [B1]
Level-marked (5–6 marks).

questions.prompt: Explain how phytochrome allows plants to detect day length and control germination. (6)
questions.solution:
Phytochrome exists in two interconvertible forms, Pr and Pfr [B1]
Pr absorbs red light (660 nm) and becomes Pfr [B1]
Pfr absorbs far-red light (730 nm) and becomes Pr; Pfr slowly reverts in darkness [B1]
Ratio of Pfr : Pr shows length of the dark period [B1]
Pfr acts as a signal (transcription factor) switching on genes, e.g. for germination [B1]
Seeds under a leaf canopy receive mostly far-red light, so don't germinate [B1]
Level-marked (5–6 marks).

questions.prompt: Describe experiments that show auxin causes phototropism in coleoptiles. (6)
hints: Remove the tip; mica barriers; agar blocks.
questions.solution:
Coleoptiles lit from one side bend towards light [B1]
Removing the tip stops bending, so tip is the source of the signal [B1]
Covering the tip with foil stops bending, so tip detects light [B1]
Mica barrier on the shaded side stops bending — signal moves down the shaded side [B1]
Agar block that held tips placed on one side of a decapitated coleoptile causes bending away — chemical signal [B1]
Auxin concentration measured higher on shaded side [B1]
Level-marked (5–6 marks).

questions.prompt: Adrenaline cannot cross cell membranes. Describe how it causes liver cells to raise blood glucose concentration. (3)
questions.solution:
Adrenaline binds to receptors on the cell surface membrane [B1]
Activates adenylyl cyclase to make cyclic AMP (second messenger) [B1]
cAMP activates protein kinases, which activate glycogen phosphorylase to break glycogen into glucose [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how insulin lowers blood glucose concentration. (3)
questions.solution:
Insulin binds to receptors on liver and muscle cells [B1]
More glucose transporter proteins inserted into membranes, so more glucose enters cells [B1]
Activates enzymes converting glucose to glycogen (glycogenesis) / increases respiration [B1]

questions.prompt: Compare how steroid hormones and peptide hormones affect target cells. (3)
questions.solution:
Steroid hormones are lipid-soluble and diffuse through the membrane; peptide hormones cannot [B1]
Steroids bind receptors inside the cell; peptides bind receptors on the surface [B1]
Steroid–receptor complex acts as a transcription factor; peptides act via second messengers [B1]

questions.prompt: Which combination of auxin and cytokinin gives the fastest growth of side (lateral) buds? (1)
questions.solution: Low auxin and high cytokinin [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why removing the tip of a shoot makes the plant bushier. (1)
questions.solution: Removes the source of auxin, so lateral buds are no longer inhibited and grow [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the plant growth substance that causes stomatal closure in drought. (1)
questions.solution: Abscisic acid (ABA) [B1]

questions.prompt: Some auxins can pass through cell membranes. Explain how these auxins could affect enzyme synthesis, by comparison with how oestrogen acts on human cells. (3)
hints: Hormone–receptor complex as a transcription factor.
questions.solution:
Both diffuse through the cell membrane [B1]
Bind to a receptor in the cytoplasm / nucleus, forming a hormone–receptor complex [B1]
Complex acts as a transcription factor, binding to promoters and changing transcription of genes for enzymes [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how oestrogen stimulates transcription of target genes. (3)
questions.solution:
Oestrogen diffuses through the membrane (lipid-soluble) [B1]
Binds to an oestrogen receptor, changing its shape so it is released from an inhibitor [B1]
Receptor complex enters the nucleus and binds to DNA, helping RNA polymerase transcribe the gene [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how gibberellin brings about germination in barley seeds. (3)
questions.solution:
Seed absorbs water; embryo releases gibberellin [B1]
Gibberellin switches on genes for amylase in the aleurone layer [B1]
Amylase hydrolyses starch in the endosperm to maltose / glucose for respiration and growth [B1]

questions.prompt:
Lettuce seeds were exposed to flashes of red (R) and far-red (FR) light. Germination (mean of 50 seeds ± SD): R 45 (±4); R, FR 5 (±2); R, FR, R 45 (±5); R, FR, R, FR 10 (±4).

Analyse these data. (4)
hints: What does the last flash decide?
questions.solution:
The final flash determines germination: R last → high germination; FR last → low [B1]
Red light converts Pr to Pfr, which stimulates germination [B1]
Far-red converts Pfr back to Pr, inhibiting germination [B1]
SDs don't overlap between R-last and FR-last groups, so the differences are likely significant [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why small seeds such as lettuce only germinate when exposed to light, and why this is an advantage. (4)
questions.solution:
Small seeds have limited food stores [B1]
Need to photosynthesise soon after germination [B1]
Germinating only in red-rich light (not under a canopy, which transmits far-red) ensures enough light [B1]
Pfr produced in red light triggers germination [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why a long-day plant fails to flower if a short period of darkness interrupts a long day, but flowers if a flash of light interrupts a long night. (4)
questions.solution:
Plants measure the length of the dark period (via Pfr levels) [B1]
A long-day plant flowers when the night is short, so Pfr levels remain high [B1]
A dark break during the day has little effect on Pfr [B1]
A flash of red light during the night converts Pr to Pfr, so the night is effectively short and the plant flowers [B1]

questions.prompt:
(i) Name the region of the brain that controls heart rate. (1)
(ii) Name the neurotransmitter released by the sympathetic nervous system at the heart. (1)
questions.solution:
(i) Medulla oblongata [B1]
(ii) Noradrenaline [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe the effects of the sympathetic and parasympathetic nervous systems on heart rate. (2)
questions.solution:
Sympathetic releases noradrenaline at the SAN, increasing heart rate [B1]
Parasympathetic (vagus nerve) releases acetylcholine, decreasing heart rate [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how a rise in blood pressure is detected and corrected. (2)
questions.solution:
Baroreceptors in the aorta / carotid arteries detect the rise and send impulses to the medulla [B1]
Medulla sends more impulses along the parasympathetic nerve, slowing heart rate and lowering blood pressure [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the retinal cell that passes impulses from rods and cones to ganglion cells. (1)
questions.solution: Bipolar cell [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the cells whose axons form the optic nerve. (1)
questions.solution: Ganglion cells [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the region of the retina with the highest density of cones. (1)
questions.solution: Fovea [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain the role of rhodopsin in generating a nerve impulse in a bipolar cell when light falls on the retina. (3)
questions.solution:
Light breaks rhodopsin into retinal and opsin (bleaching) [B1]
Na⁺ channels in the rod cell membrane close; rod hyperpolarises [B1]
Rod stops releasing inhibitory neurotransmitter (glutamate), so bipolar cell depolarises and generates an impulse [B1]

questions.prompt: Compare rods and cones. (3)
questions.solution:
Rods are more sensitive to low light; cones need bright light [B1]
Cones give colour vision (three types); rods give black-and-white vision [B1]
Cones give high visual acuity (one cone per bipolar cell); rods show convergence and low acuity [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why it takes several minutes to see clearly after walking from bright sunlight into a dark room. (3)
questions.solution:
In bright light, most rhodopsin is bleached / broken down [B1]
Rods can't respond until rhodopsin is resynthesised from retinal and opsin [B1]
Resynthesis takes time (and ATP), so sensitivity increases gradually [B1]

questions.prompt:
People sat in darkness and the dimmest light they could see was recorded over 30 minutes, using a blue-green (500 nm) light and a red (620 nm) light. For 500 nm, sensitivity improved quickly at first, then improved a second time after about 8 minutes, eventually detecting very dim light. For 620 nm, sensitivity improved only in the first 8 minutes and then stayed constant. Rods are most sensitive around 500 nm and are not sensitive to 620 nm; cones respond to both.

Analyse these data to explain the results. (6)
hints: Which receptor responds to red light?
questions.solution:
The first fast improvement is due to cones adapting (cone pigments resynthesised quickly) [B1]
The second phase at 500 nm is due to rods, as rhodopsin is resynthesised more slowly [B1]
Rods are more sensitive than cones, so lower intensities detected after rods adapt [B1]
Rods don't absorb 620 nm light, so only cones detect red light [B1]
So no second phase at 620 nm; minimum intensity stays higher [B1]
Rod convergence / summation explains their greater sensitivity [B1]
Level-marked (5–6 marks).

questions.prompt: Explain how the three types of cone allow us to see a wide range of colours, and why some people are red–green colour blind. (6)
questions.solution:
There are three types of cone, each with a different iodopsin pigment [B1]
Each absorbs a different range of wavelengths (blue, green, red), with overlap [B1]
The brain interprets the relative stimulation of each type as a colour [B1]
Different combinations give all perceived colours [B1]
Colour blindness: a faulty allele means one cone pigment is missing / altered [B1]
The genes are on the X chromosome, so it is more common in males [B1]
Level-marked (5–6 marks).

questions.prompt: Explain why we see more detail in the centre of our vision but can detect dimmer light in our peripheral vision. (6)
questions.solution:
The fovea contains only cones, densely packed [B1]
Each cone connects to its own bipolar cell [B1]
So the brain receives separate signals from close points — high acuity [B1]
The periphery has mostly rods [B1]
Many rods converge onto one bipolar cell, so signals summate to reach threshold in dim light [B1]
But detail is lost because the brain can't tell which rod was stimulated [B1]
Level-marked (5–6 marks).

questions.prompt: Name the parts of the nephron where glucose is normally present in the filtrate. (1)
questions.solution: Bowman's capsule and proximal convoluted tubule (none left after the PCT) [B1]

questions.prompt: Name the part of the nephron where most glucose is reabsorbed. (1)
questions.solution: Proximal convoluted tubule [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why glucose may appear in the urine of a person with untreated diabetes. (1)
questions.solution: Blood glucose is so high that the carrier proteins in the PCT are saturated, so not all glucose is reabsorbed [B1]

questions.prompt:
Furosemide reduces the active transport of sodium ions out of the ascending limb of the loop of Henle.

Explain how this increases urine production. (4)
hints: The loop creates a gradient in the medulla.
questions.solution:
Fewer Na⁺ ions pumped into the medulla [B1]
So the water potential of the medulla is less negative / not as low [B1]
Less water reabsorbed by osmosis from the descending limb and collecting duct [B1]
More water stays in the filtrate, so more dilute urine is produced [B1]

questions.prompt: Describe how ADH controls the water content of the blood when a person is dehydrated. (4)
questions.solution:
Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect the low water potential of the blood [B1]
Posterior pituitary releases more ADH [B1]
ADH causes more aquaporins to be inserted into collecting duct membranes [B1]
More water reabsorbed by osmosis, so less, more concentrated urine [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why desert mammals have long loops of Henle. (4)
questions.solution:
Longer loop allows more Na⁺ / Cl⁻ to be pumped into the medulla [B1]
Creating a lower water potential in the medulla [B1]
More water reabsorbed from the collecting duct by osmosis [B1]
Very concentrated urine, conserving water [B1]

questions.prompt:
In a gel, a 4 kb marker moved 20 mm and a 2 kb marker moved 35 mm. A fragment moved 27 mm.

Estimate the size of the fragment and explain why your answer is only an estimate. (1)
hints: It lies between the two markers.
questions.solution: About 3 kb; the relationship between distance and size is not linear (logarithmic), so interpolation is approximate [B1]

questions.prompt: A child's DNA profile has a band not present in the mother's profile. What does this show? (1)
hints: Each band is inherited from one parent.
questions.solution: The band was inherited from the father [B1]

questions.prompt: Why is a DNA ladder (marker) run alongside samples in gel electrophoresis? (1)
hints: It contains fragments of known size.
questions.solution: To estimate the size of unknown fragments by comparison with fragments of known length [B1]

questions.prompt:
In an investigation into antigen presentation, endothelial cells were irradiated before being cultured with T lymphocytes. Irradiation stops cells dividing.

Explain why this was done, given that cell division was measured using radioactive thymidine. (2)
hints: Thymidine is taken up by dividing cells.
questions.solution:
Prevents the endothelial cells dividing / taking up radioactive thymidine [B1]
So any radioactivity measured comes only from dividing T lymphocytes [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why radioactive thymidine can be used to measure the rate of cell division. (2)
hints: Which molecule is copied before division?
questions.solution:
Thymidine is a nucleotide (base) used to make DNA [B1]
It is incorporated when DNA replicates before division, so more radioactivity = more division [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why cells were washed thoroughly before radioactivity was measured. (2)
hints: Some thymidine is not inside cells.
questions.solution:
To remove radioactive thymidine not taken up by cells [B1]
So only thymidine incorporated into DNA is measured — prevents overestimating division [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why T lymphocytes were cultured both with and without an antigen. (2)
questions.solution:
To act as a control / show what happens without antigen [B1]
So any increase in division can be attributed to the antigen [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain the purpose of a positive control in an investigation, using an example. (2)
questions.solution:
A positive control uses something known to give a result, to show the method can detect an effect [B1]
e.g. a substance known to make T cells divide (such as Con A), or a known reducing sugar in a food test [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why investigations often use several different antigens rather than one. (2)
questions.solution:
To show whether the effect occurs generally or only with one antigen [B1]
Allows comparison / increases validity of conclusions [B1]

questions.prompt:
A low-density lipoprotein (LDL) is a sphere with a diameter of 22 nm.

Calculate its volume using V = 4/3 πr³ (π = 3.14). (2)
Calculate the surface area to volume ratio of a cell modelled as a cube of side 4 µm. (2)
questions.solution:
SA = 96 µm², V = 64 µm³ [M1]
Ratio = 1.5 : 1 [A1]

questions.prompt: A high-density lipoprotein (HDL) has a diameter of 8 nm. Calculate how many times greater the volume of a 22 nm LDL is. (2)
questions.solution:
Ratio of radii = 11 ÷ 4 = 2.75 [M1]
2.75³ = 20.8 times greater [A1]

questions.prompt:
A 10 µm scale bar on a micrograph measures 25 mm.

Calculate the magnification and give your answer in standard form. (2)

A 5 µm scale bar measures 40 mm. A stoma on the same image measures 56 mm long.

Calculate the actual length of the stoma. (2)
A scale bar labelled 2 µm measures 18 mm. Calculate the magnification. (2)
A stoma in a GM plant is 5.4 µm wide; in a non-modified plant it is 3.6 µm wide. How many times wider is the GM stoma? (1)
A leaf section of 0.2 mm² has 34 stomata. Calculate the stomatal density per mm². (1)
questions.solution: 170 stomata mm⁻² [B1]

questions.prompt: The area of an open stoma is 30 µm² and a partly closed one is 12 µm². Calculate the percentage decrease in area. (1)
questions.solution: 60 % decrease [B1]

questions.prompt:
An experimental drug for Ebola was given to infected monkeys on day 1, day 3 or day 5 after infection. All 6 untreated monkeys died. Survival was 6/6 for day-1 treatment, 5/6 for day 3 and 4/6 for day 5. Severe side effects were seen in 11, 7 and 3 animals respectively in larger trial groups.

Assess the effectiveness of the drug. (4)
questions.solution:
Drug increases survival compared with untreated controls (0 % survived) [B1]
Earlier treatment is more effective (100 % on day 1 vs 67 % on day 5) [B1]
But earlier treatment caused more severe side effects [B1]
Small sample sizes; monkeys may not respond like humans [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why drugs are first tested on cells and animals before being tested on humans, and the purpose of each phase of clinical trials. (4)
questions.solution:
Cell/animal tests check for toxicity before humans are exposed [B1]
Phase 1: small group of healthy volunteers — safety and dosage [B1]
Phase 2: small group of patients — effectiveness and side effects [B1]
Phase 3: large group of patients, often double-blind against placebo / existing drug [B1]

questions.prompt: Discuss the ethical issues of testing an untrialled drug on patients during an outbreak of a deadly disease. (4)
questions.solution:
May save lives when no other treatment exists [B1]
Unknown side effects could harm patients [B1]
Patients may not be able to give informed consent when very ill [B1]
Is it fair to give a placebo / deny treatment to a control group? Limited supplies — who gets it? [B1]

questions.prompt:
Rabbits with ARDS were given compound A, compound B, both A and B, or natural surfactant. Over two hours, the Carrico index rose most with both compounds together, almost reaching that of natural surfactant. Compound A alone gave a small rise; B alone gave a moderate rise. Alveolar expansion followed the same pattern.

Assess the potential use of these compounds to treat ARDS in human babies. (6)
hints: Compare each treatment with the natural surfactant.
questions.solution:

Almost as effective as natural surfactant — could be an alternative [B1]
Compounds may work together / have a synergistic effect [B1]
Each alone was less effective [B1]
Only tested for 2 hours — long-term effects / side effects unknown [B1]

Increase in peak flow suggests airways are less constricted [B1]

Small sample of 40; may not be representative [B1]
Short trial — long-term effects and side effects unknown [B1]

Need statistical significance and larger phase 3 trials before approval [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain how the scientific community validates new findings, using the example of a new treatment for a lung disease. (6)
questions.solution:
Results are written up and submitted to a scientific journal [B1]
Peer review by other experts checks methods, data and conclusions [B1]
Published so others can see the methods and repeat the work [B1]
Other groups repeat the study to check reproducibility [B1]
Results discussed at conferences; conflicting evidence considered [B1]
Large clinical trials before the treatment is approved [B1]

A log scale fits them on one graph and shows exponential growth as a straight line [B1]

questions.prompt:
In an investigation, phagocytosis by macrophages increased with incubation time and with the concentration of bacteria, but levelled off at high concentrations. Analyse these data to explain the factors affecting phagocytosis. (6)
hints: Why does an ATP inhibitor reduce phagocytosis?
questions.solution:
More bacteria increases collisions / binding, so more phagocytosis [B1]
Levels off as macrophage receptors / capacity are saturated [B1]
More time allows more bacteria to be engulfed [B1]
Lung macrophages are more active — they are adapted to meet pathogens frequently [B1]
Phagocytosis needs ATP (for actin / pseudopodia / vesicle movement), so an ATP synthase inhibitor reduces it [B1]
Limitations: need repeats / statistical tests / standard deviations [B1]

questions.prompt: Devise an investigation to compare the rate of phagocytosis of yeast cells by white blood cells at different temperatures. (6)

Incubate samples at a range of temperatures (e.g. 20–45 °C) in water baths [B1]
After a set time, stop the reaction (cold / fixative) [B1]
Count the number of yeast cells inside 100 white blood cells under a microscope [B1]
Control volume, concentrations, time, pH [B1]
Repeat and calculate means; plot rate against temperature [B1]

questions.prompt:

questions.solution:
White cell count tripled (200 % increase) [B1]
Neutrophils rise first — non-specific response / phagocytosis [B1]
Lymphocytes rise later — specific response takes time [B1]
Clonal selection and expansion of B and T cells [B1]
Plasma cells produce antibodies; memory cells formed [B1]
Count returns to normal as the infection is cleared [B1]
Level-marked (5–6 marks).

HIF-2 gives a longer-term response, e.g. more red blood cells (EPO) / new blood vessels [B1]

questions.prompt: Explain why athletes sometimes train at high altitude before competitions. (2)

More red blood cells, so more oxygen carried when competing at sea level [B1]
